items.descriptionOriginal: You wake up and your nose is the first thing to tell you what the air is like. One side is blocked, then the other. There is a dull pressure behind your cheeks, your eyes itch, and the sky outside is the colour of dishwater. You open the AQI app and it says "severe" . Then the questions begin. Is this my sinusitis flaring up? An allergy? Or is it just the smog? Should I reach for that decongestant spray in the drawer? Do I need a doctor, or will this pass when the air clears? If you live in Delhi NCR with chronic sinusitis or allergic rhinitis, you may know this morning well. Your nose was inflamed long before the first particle of smog arrived, and now you're left guessing, often with whatever is nearest to hand. Dr M. Shantanu, an ENT specialist in Delhi, says that guesswork is where people go wrong. "Not every blocked nose is sinusitis," he says, and treating it as if it were can backfire. Here are his answers to the questions people ask most on bad air days, as a field guide for when the sky turns grey. It does not replace a consultation with your own doctor. Why smog hits sinus and allergy patients harder Why does a high AQI make a blocked nose worse? "Think of the nose as a security checkpoint. Mucus and tiny hair-like structures called cilia catch dust, allergens, and microorganisms, while the sinuses rely on that same system to drain," he explains. People living with chronic sinusitis may experience increased congestion, facial pressure and reduced smell during periods of severe air pollution. Photograph: (TNIE) When fine particles slip in, they irritate the lining and set off inflammation. The swelling narrows the small passages linking the sinuses to the nose. Drainage slows, and an old problem feels brand new. Dr Shantanu points to research linking particulate exposure with chronic rhinosinusitis and with greater severity. If your congestion, sneezing, facial pressure, postnasal drip, headaches or dulled sense of smell keep flaring when the air is bad, he says, take it as a cue to identify your triggers. Which pollutants are the troublemakers? PM2.5 and PM10, particles measuring 2.5 and 10 micrometres or less, top his list. They arrive via vehicle exhaust, construction dust, industrial emissions and smoke. Traffic-related nitrogen dioxide, a gas produced mainly by burning fuel, adds to the irritation. "If you live or work near a building site, expect more sneezing and a runnier nose, especially if you have allergies," he says. Is it sinusitis, allergy, or just pollution irritation? The three overlap, so Dr Shantanu reads the pattern. Pollution irritation burns, blocks, and makes you sneeze during or after exposure, usually without fever. Allergic rhinitis brings sneezing, an itchy nose, watery eyes and a runny nose after contact with pollen, dust mites or pet dander. Sinusitis means congestion, facial pressure, reduced smell and nasal discharge, sometimes with fever. Chronic rhinosinusitis generally means symptoms lasting at least 12 weeks. Pollution and allergy can also feed each other, so your symptoms may refuse to sit in one box. Can a smoggy day give me a sinus infection? Not automatically, he says. " Pollution can make symptoms harder to control in people who already have a nasal or sinus condition." Allergic rhinitis can cause repeated sneezing, itchy eyes, nasal irritation and a runny nose when pollution levels rise. Photograph: ( TNIE ) Viral infections, especially colds, are the most common cause of acute sinus infections. Mucus colour alone cannot confirm a bacterial infection. Your cause, the duration of symptoms, and a clinical examination should decide treatment, because not every blocked nose needs antibiotics. What does it do to daily life? Persistent congestion, sleep broken by difficulty breathing through the nose, a foggy head, repeated flare-ups and allergies that are harder to manage. Dr Shantanu adds that not everyone who breathes dirty air develops chronic sinusitis . Genetics, allergies, nasal anatomy, infections, and smoking all shape individual risk. His survival guide for a high-AQI day Where do I start? Check the AQI before you plan anything outdoors. When it is poor, cut both the length and the intensity of outdoor exercise, especially near busy roads and construction sites. Saline nasal sprays and rinses can help clear mucus and trapped irritants, provided sterile, distilled or boiled-and-cooled water is used. Photograph: ( Dreamstime ) Keep a note of whether your symptoms worsen on high-pollution days. That record helps an ENT specialist pin down your triggers. Reduce smoke and chemical fumes at home too, and follow workplace safety measures if your job is dusty. Does a mask really help? A well-fitting N95 worn outdoors can cut inhalation of many airborne particles. It is not a force field, though. It does not remove every harmful gas, so he treats it as one layer of protection and not the whole answer. Ordinary cloth or surgical masks do far less against fine particles. How do I keep my home air cleaner? Keep windows and doors shut when the air outside is bad, and run a correctly sized HEPA purifier if you have one. HEPA air purifiers can help reduce indoor particulate pollution, while limiting incense, cigarette smoke and other indoor pollutants. Photograph: ( India Today ) Skip cigarettes, incense, and other indoor smoke. Open up the house only when the air outside is cleaner than the air inside. How do I rinse my nose safely? Saline sprays or rinses clear mucus and irritants, so they suit the end of a day spent outside. The water is what makes it safe: distilled, sterile, or boiled and cooled. Never untreated tap water. Clean the device as its instructions say. Can I reach for a decongestant spray? Dr Shantanu advises against self-medicating with them, because some cause rebound congestion when used longer than recommended. If symptoms are frequent, get them assessed instead of treating them again and again with over-the-counter medicines. Do fluids and sleep help? They support general wellbeing, and he recommends both. But they do not prevent pollution-related sinus inflammation on their own, so they belong beside the steps above, not instead of them. Delhi NCR's air pollution, driven by vehicle emissions, construction dust and smoke, can make breathing uncomfortable and aggravate existing nasal and sinus conditions. Photograph: ( Conway Airmen ) The goal of the whole routine is to reduce irritation and keep symptoms manageable, not to promise they will never appear. And home remedies? Warm compresses, rest, and saline rinses can ease a viral infection but cannot reliably clear a bacterial one. If symptoms continue, see a doctor. When to see an ENT specialist How do I know it has gone beyond a bad air day? Occasional sneezing often settles once you leave the trigger behind. Persistent or recurring symptoms deserve attention. Book a consultation if you have: congestion or facial pressure that will not improve repeated episodes of suspected sinusitis a persistent loss or reduction of smell blockage mainly on one side symptoms that disturb sleep or daily activities persistent or recurrent headache or ear heaviness What will the specialist do? An ENT specialist can tell pollution irritation apart from allergic rhinitis, recurrent sinusitis, nasal polyps or structural problems like a deviated septum. Saline nasal sprays and rinses can help clear mucus and trapped irritants, provided sterile, distilled or boiled-and-cooled water is used. Photograph: ( AI-Generated image ) That can mean reviewing your symptoms, exposure history and past treatments, examining your nasal passages, identifying allergy triggers, and advising on tests or imaging when clinically indicated. Treatment follows the cause, from saline irrigation to nasal medication or allergy management. Antibiotics are not routine for every episode, and surgery is for selected cases only. Which symptoms are urgent? Swelling or redness around the eyes, vision changes, a severe or unusual headache, confusion, or any rapidly worsening symptoms. Go to a doctor straight away. The one-breath version Check the AQI before you step out. Wear a snug N95 if you must. Keep indoor air clean. Rinse with safe water. Note whether your symptoms follow the smog. "None of this guarantees your sinuses will stay quiet. But if symptoms linger, recur or worsen, take that record to an ENT specialist. But most importantly, know that help is always available and self-medication is not a solution," Dr Shantanu says.

items.descriptionOriginal: On a Saturday morning in October 2026, seven Pune residents gathered at Madhavrao Scindia Garden beside the Mula River. Across the water, two fishers steered their boat past a thick patch of trees. The residents had brought smartphones and measuring tapes. They were there to document trees that people might pass every day without giving them much thought. They photographed individual trees, noted their species, measured the circumference of their trunks and recorded their locations on a phone app. Each entry added another piece to a growing map of Pune's riverbank greenery. It may seem like a small weekend exercise. But for these volunteers, knowing exactly which trees grow where could make a difference when the city decides what to build next. Why are Pune residents counting trees? The volunteers belong to Pune River Revival (PRR), a citizen group that began mapping trees more systematically in 2024, amid concerns about the ₹4,727-crore Pune Riverfront Development Project. The plan includes promenades, recreational spaces and other construction along the Mula-Mutha riverbanks. The group wanted a clearer record of the trees and other living things already thriving there. That meant going beyond counting trunks. "We started organizing the tree mapping exercise systematically in 2024," volunteer Raghunandan Patil told Mongabay. Earlier, he explained, the group had mapped trees by hand but lacked the technical knowledge to document them properly. Today, volunteers use iNaturalist, an app on which people can upload photographs and locations of plants and animals. It helps them identify species and build a record that others can consult. During mapping walks, volunteers spread out across stretches of the riverbank, taking photographs and measurements as they go. Every entry helps answer an important question: if a patch of greenery disappears tomorrow, will anyone know what was there? More than 500 trees faced removal. Residents got to work. That question became urgent on Ganeshkhind Road, where plans to widen a busy stretch threatened 529 trees , including mature trees believed to be decades old. When residents approached PRR, volunteers documented over 500 trees within a month. The records helped put names, numbers and locations to trees that people feared losing. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Pune Tree Mappers PRR (@punetreemapping.rivers) The concern spread beyond the mapping group. On 18 and 19 April 2026, residents, artists and environmentalists came together for tree mapping, live painting and music, drawing attention to the proposed widening of the road between Sancheti Hospital and Savitribai Phule Pune University. Under an earlier proposal, 469 trees were to be transplanted and 60 cut down. Environmentalists questioned whether older trees could survive being moved. "I grew up with these trees and they are part of every Punekar's heritage," artist Janaki Gandhi told Pune Mirror. "Through art, we want people to see each tree as a living identity, not just an obstacle in a road plan." Citizens also raised objections and pushed for changes to the road design. By September 2026, the Pune Municipal Corporation had revised its proposal, reducing the number of trees marked for removal from 529 to 33. That meant 496 trees could be spared under the revised plan. The change came through wider citizen action and efforts by environmental groups. Mapping helped document what was at stake and gave residents another way to make their case. What can a sacred grove teach a growing city? Along the rivers, PRR has also drawn attention to Ram-Mula Devrai, a sacred grove where the Ram and Mula rivers meet. A devrai is a forest patch traditionally protected by local communities because it is believed to be the dwelling place of a village deity. In a busy city, it can also offer shelter to plants, birds and other wildlife. Reports cited by Mongabay record around 1,000 heritage trees and at least 450 species of plants and animals in the grove. Among them are 160 bird species, as well as the Bengal monitor lizard and checkered keelback snake. During a mapping exercise, volunteers divide themselves across assigned stretches of the riverbank. Each person records observations directly on the platform. Photograph: (Pune River Revival-Via-Free Press Journal) To help more people discover this place, volunteers organised butterfly and insect walks, tree-painting competitions and other activities. They also suggested ways visitors could enjoy the space while protecting its trees. Their efforts showed how people could explore and appreciate a natural space while keeping its greenery intact. From riverbanks to hilltops, more people are joining in Elsewhere in Pune, citizens are building similar records. On Chatushrungi, Taljai and ARAI hills, the Green Hills Group uses an app called TrackMyTree to record saplings, their locations, species and caretakers. Revisiting those records can tell volunteers which trees are surviving and where they need attention. Along the Mula, PRR and JeevitNadi volunteers have also used ConnecTree, a tool developed by the Pune Knowledge Cluster, to document riverbank trees and saplings . View this post on Instagram A post shared by Civic Sense Task Force (CSTF) PCMC Pune (@civicsensetaskforce) Pune Municipal Corporation says it conducts a tree census every five years. But citizen groups believe accessible, regularly updated records are important too, especially when residents want to understand how a proposed project may affect their neighbourhood. Back at the river, the work still comes down to a photograph, a measurement and a location saved on a phone. The same simple steps the seven volunteers took that October morning could one day give residents a record to point to when an old tree is marked for removal. And as Pune continues to grow, these records give its residents something valuable: a clearer picture of the trees around them and a stronger voice in deciding how to protect them. Sources: 'How citizen scientists are mapping Pune's trees, with hopes of a greener future' : By Stephin Thomas, Published on 30 October 2026 'Pune Citizens Take Geotagging Of Green Cover Into Their Own Hands' : By Urban Acres, Published on 21 July 2025 'Citizens Launch Weekend Art and Music Protest to Save Ganeshkhind Road Trees' : By Chaitraly Deshmukh, Published on 18 April 2026

Ο προβληματισμός της δεν φτάνει ως συμβουλή αλλά ως άδεια: να νιώθει ημιτελής και ολοκληρωμένη ταυτόχρονα, να σταματήσει να περιμένει…
items.descriptionOriginal: At twenty-two, Haile Thomas sat with a question most of us quietly carry for decades: what do I do with all of this existence? Rather than answer it, she did something braver -- she wrote her way into the uncertainty itself. Her reflection arrives not as advice but as permission: to feel incomplete and whole at the same time, to stop waiting for the map that will never come. She offers a quietly radical image of identity -- that growing up is less about finding yourself than noticing "the entity that gets dressed," the spaciousness beneath every costume we try on and discard. There is no finish line in her telling, only transformations meeting us in the moments we least expect. "Growing up is a never ending journey," she writes -- and somehow that lands not as defeat but as relief. What she offers, finally, is not wisdom so much as weather: a loosening, a liquefying of the hard certainties we grip when life refuses to hold still.

items.descriptionOriginal: Μπορεί η ευτυχία να καλλιεργηθεί; Η περίπτωση του βουδιστή μοναχού Yongey Mingyur Rinpoche έχει κινήσει εδώ και χρόνια το ενδιαφέρον των νευροεπιστημόνων, καθώς μελέτες που εξέτασαν τον εγκέφαλό του κατά τη διάρκεια διαλογισμού κατέγραψαν εντυπωσιακά πρότυπα εγκεφαλικής δραστηριότητας. Συγκεκριμένα, οι απεικονίσεις έδειξαν ασυνήθιστα επίπεδα ενεργοποίησης στον αριστερό προμετωπιαίο φλοιό, μια περιοχή που σχετίζεται με θετικά συναισθήματα όπως η ευτυχία , ο ενθουσιασμός και η χαρά. Ο ίδιος δεν υπόσχεται κάποια εύκολη συνταγή. Αντίθετα, προτείνει να δοκιμάσουμε τα δικά του 9 μαθήματα ζωής, για μεγαλύτερη ικανοποίηση. Να μην προσπαθούμε να γεμίσουμε κάθε κενό Ένα από τα βασικά μηνύματα του Mingyur αφορά τη σύγχρονη ανάγκη για συνεχή διέγερση. «Όπως λέει ο Δαλάι Λάμα, σήμερα τα έχουμε όλα με το πάτημα ενός κουμπιού. Έτσι, όταν αρχίζουμε να νιώθουμε μοναξιά ή ανία, προσπαθούμε να προστατευτούμε με οτιδήποτε: παγωτό, κινητό, καφέ» , λέει χαρακτηριστικά στον Guardian. «Προσπαθούμε να ξεφύγουμε από αυτά τα συναισθήματα, όμως κατά κάποιον τρόπο κρύβουν σοφία. Το σημαντικό είναι να μείνουμε μαζί τους, να τα αποδεχτούμε και να τα χρησιμοποιήσουμε ως αφορμή για εξερεύνηση». Να αποδεχόμαστε τις αλλαγές Το 2011, ο Mingyur εγκατέλειψε το μοναστήρι του μέσα στη νύχτα, με σκοπό να ζήσει για ένα διάστημα ως περιπλανώμενος γιόγκι. Λίγες εβδομάδες αργότερα υπέστη σοβαρή τροφική δηλητηρίαση και πέρασε ημέρες εξαντλημένος από τον πόνο. Σήμερα περιγράφει εκείνη την εμπειρία ως καθοριστική για να κατανοήσει βαθύτερα την έννοια της εγκατάλειψης του ελέγχου. Όπως υποστηρίζει, δεν χρειάζεται κανείς να περάσει από μια ακραία δοκιμασία για να εξοικειωθεί με την αλλαγή. «Η σύγχρονη ζωή είναι γεμάτη περιπέτειες. Όταν γίνεσαι 18, όταν ξεκινάς μια νέα δουλειά ή μια νέα σχέση, όλα αυτά είναι ευκαιρίες για αλλαγή», λέει. Ακόμη και μικρές διαφοροποιήσεις στην καθημερινότητα, όπως μια νέα διαδρομή προς το σπίτι, μια διαφορετική δραστηριότητα ή μια καινούργια εμπειρία, μπορούν να βοηθήσουν κάποιον να γίνει πιο άνετος απέναντι στο άγνωστο. Δεν χρειαζόμαστε απαραίτητα σιωπή για να βρούμε γαλήνη Ο ίδιος παραδέχεται ότι όταν πρωτογνώρισε τον διαλογισμό , η αντίδρασή του κάθε άλλο παρά ενθουσιώδης ήταν. «Βαρέθηκα την πρώτη φορά που έμαθα διαλογισμό. Είπα: “Σήμερα αναπνοή. Αύριο πάλι αναπνοή. Όλη την υπόλοιπη εβδομάδα, αναπνοή. Αυτό είναι ανόητο”», θυμάται. Στη συνέχεια, όμως, κατανόησε ότι ο διαλογισμός δεν απαιτεί απαραίτητα απόλυτη ησυχία ή ιδανικές συνθήκες . «Για τον διαλογισμό χρειάζεται να ξέρεις δύο πράγματα. Πρώτον, μπορείς να διαλογιστείς οποτεδήποτε, οπουδήποτε, με οτιδήποτε. Δεύτερον, πρέπει να υπάρχει ένα δημιουργικό στοιχείο. Τα πάντα μπορούν να γίνουν φίλοι του διαλογισμού». Αυτό σημαίνει ότι ακόμη και ο θόρυβος της κίνησης, μια συζήτηση στο διπλανό δωμάτιο ή άλλοι περισπασμοί μπορούν να γίνουν σημεία εστίασης αντί για εμπόδια. Να αξιοποιήσουμε 3 βασικούς πυλώνες Ο Mingyur περιγράφει τρεις βασικούς άξονες της θιβετιανής βουδιστικής παράδοσης: οπτική, διαλογισμό και εφαρμογή . «Η οπτική είναι η νοοτροπία. Πιστεύουμε ότι όλοι έχουν έναν εσωτερικό ουρανό, τις ποιότητες της επίγνωσης, της αγάπης, της συμπόνιας και της σοφίας. Εξασκούμε τον διαλογισμό και μετά εφαρμόζουμε όσα μάθαμε, χτίζοντας νέες συνήθειες», εξηγεί. Για τον ίδιο, η αλλαγή της οπτικής απαιτεί εξάσκηση. «Είναι εύκολο να πει κανείς “οι άνθρωποι δεν είναι καλοί”. Υπάρχουν όμως πολλές σπουδαίες ιδιότητες σε πολλούς ανθρώπους. Αν αρχίσεις να τις βλέπεις, θα εμφανίζονται περισσότερο. Είναι συνήθεια: πρέπει να το κάνεις ξανά και ξανά και τότε αλλάζεις». Μια απλή καθημερινή άσκηση θα μπορούσε να είναι η συνειδητή αναγνώριση θετικών χαρακτηριστικών στους ανθρώπους γύρω μας, ακόμα και σε εκείνους που μας ενοχλούν περισσότερο. Να νιώθουμε ευγνωμοσύνη, αλλά όχι γενικά και αόριστα Η ευγνωμοσύνη, σύμφωνα με τον Mingyur, δεν χρειάζεται να παίρνει τη μορφή μιας γενικής λίστας. «Εκτιμώ ότι έχω τις αισθήσεις μου, ότι υπάρχει μια στέγη πάνω από το κεφάλι μου, ότι έχω τουλάχιστον έναν ή δύο φίλους ή συγγενείς» , λέει. «Όταν αρχίσουμε να εκτιμούμε αυτά τα πράγματα, αρχίζουμε να εκτιμούμε την ποιότητα της ζωής μας και όλα όσα υπάρχουν γύρω μας». Η ουσία βρίσκεται στο συγκεκριμένο: σε μια άνετη καρέκλα, σε μια ήρεμη στιγμή, σε μια καθημερινή εικόνα που συνήθως περνά απαρατήρητη. Να θυμόμαστε ότι ο πανικός είναι μόνο ένα σύννεφο στον ουρανό Ο μοναχός μιλά και για τις κρίσεις πανικού που είχε σε νεαρή ηλικία. «Όταν άρχισα να μαθαίνω διαλογισμό από τον πατέρα μου, τον ρώτησα πώς να τις πολεμήσω. Μου είπε: “Μην πολεμάς”», θυμάται. Όπως εξηγεί, η προσπάθεια να διώξει κάποιος τον φόβο μπορεί να τον ενισχύσει. «Δεν χρειάζεται να διώξω τον πανικό. Είναι σαν σύννεφο καταιγίδας στον ουρανό. Έρχεται και φεύγει, χωρίς να αλλάζει τον ουρανό. Πρέπει απλώς να συνδεθείς με τον εσωτερικό σου ουρανό». Σε στιγμές έντασης, προτείνει να στρέφουμε την προσοχή σε απτές αισθήσεις, όπως η θερμοκρασία ή οι ήχοι γύρω μας. Και ο θυμός η πάχνη στο γρασίδι «Αυτό που αποκαλούμε επίγνωση είναι σαν το φως του ήλιου και τα συναισθηματικά μας μοτίβα είναι σαν την πάχνη στο γρασίδι το πρωί. Όταν εμφανίζεται το φως του ήλιου, η πάχνη λιώνει αυτόματα. Δεν υπάρχει μάχη» τονίζει. Η πρότασή του είναι απλή: Πριν αντιδράσουμε, να αναγνωρίσουμε πρώτα το συναίσθημα. « Μείνε με τον θυμό . Έστω για ένα δευτερόλεπτο. Μόλις τον πιάσεις, έχεις επιλογή. Μπορεί να μεταμορφωθεί». Να μην περιμένουμε την ευτυχία στην επόμενη επιτυχία Για τον Mingyur, το κυνήγι της ευτυχίας μπορεί εύκολα να οδηγήσει στο αντίθετο αποτέλεσμα . «Η γνήσια ευτυχία έρχεται όταν αφήνουμε αυτό το αίσθημα δυσαρέσκειας, ανεπάρκειας, ότι κάτι λείπει», λέει. «Οι άνθρωποι συχνά σκέφτονται: “Θα είμαι ευτυχισμένος αν βγάλω περισσότερα χρήματα, αν μετακομίσω σε μια νέα χώρα, αν βρω μια νέα δουλειά ή αν κερδίσω το λαχείο”. Όμως αυτό αλλάζει την ευτυχία μόνο λίγο και μετά επιστρέφεις στο βασικό επίπεδο». Κατά τον ίδιο, πρακτικές όπως η συνειδητή αναπνοή, η αγάπη και η συμπόνια μπορούν σταδιακά να επηρεάσουν αυτή τη βασική αίσθηση ευεξίας . Και, τελικά, βοηθά να βοηθάμε Στο τέλος, ο Mingyur επιστρέφει σε μια πολύ απλή ιδέα: η ευτυχία δεν είναι μόνο εσωτερική υπόθεση. «Αν μπορείς πραγματικά να βοηθήσεις τους άλλους, νιώθεις ένα διαφορετικό επίπεδο ευτυχίας από αυτό που μπορεί να σου δώσει ένα παγωτό ή ένας καφές», καταλήγει. Διαβάστε επίσης Ευτυχία: Μία ψυχολόγος δίνει 5 πολύτιμες συμβουλές για να νιώσουμε χαρά όταν όλα γύρω μας είναι ζοφερά Θλίψη και αίσθημα κενού: Τι είναι το σύνδρομο της «άδειας ζωής» και πώς θα το διαχειριστούμε Γιατί το εμμονικό κυνήγι της ευτυχίας γίνεται μπούμερανγκ που εξουθενώνει και οδηγεί σε δυστυχία

items.descriptionOriginal: Low oxygen levels in the brain, or cerebral anoxia, are a leading cause of death worldwide. Patients who recover from cerebral anoxia deal with persistent neurological issues that worsen their quality of life. Building on previous work showing that brain–heart interactions can predict the severity of symptoms and survival, Diego Candia-Rivera, Sofia Carrion-Falgarona and colleagues from the Paris Brain Institute assessed whether brain–heart interactions in a rat model of severe oxygen loss can predict survival after resuscitation. The work is published in eNeuro.

items.descriptionOriginal: An Indian Village with ZERO Electricity Bill, FREE Cooking Gas & Women Own Every Home? Sounds like a fairytale? Meet Shelkewadi, Maharashtra! For 20+ years, Shelkewadi has solved problems that Indian cities still struggle with: LPG dependency, power cuts, water crisis, pollution, and waste, all without crores in budget. In this episode of Solved In India, we visit this tiny village in Karvir Taluka, Kolhapur, where barely 80 families live. They’ve built a real-life zero-waste, self-sufficient, sustainable village model that every Indian village can copy. With 60% of India’s LPG imported and a big part of it passing through the Strait of Hormuz, Shelkewadi shows what energy independence looks like at the village level. Imagine if every village in India followed this model. Would you move to a village like this? Αλλά τα παιδιά είναι παραγωγικοί δημιουργοί, οπότε τι πρέπει να γίνει με όλους αυτούς τους χάρτινους καμβάδες κατασκευών καθώς κατακλύζονται συνεχώς; Καλλιτέχνης Σ…
items.descriptionOriginal: A stick figure family, a googly-eyed monster, a happy rainbow. Children’s artwork represents how they see the world at any given age — a sweet, fleeting perspective that the adults in their lives yearn to preserve. But kids are prolific creators, so what’s to be done with all these construction paper canvases as more continuously flood in? Artist Shana Blakley came up with a creative way to save her kids’ drawings while breaking out of a rut she’d been in with her own work: She turned them into a big, colorful collage to hang in her family’s home. When she shared the result on Instagram, her comment section exploded. The idea clearly resonated with other moms, dads, and grandparents. Heirloom Collage Shana Blakley’s first kids’ artwork collage “We want to honor what our kids make,” Blakley told Nice News, adding: “Nearly every parent around the world has a growing pile of kid art, and it’s in our nature to save it. We feel guilty throwing it away, but storing it also begins to feel unsettling. There comes a time when you realize how much of it you have and you ask yourself: ‘What am I keeping this for?’” Heirloom Collage Molly Revers with her grandkids and the collages made from their artwork Shortly after posting the piece last year, she launched Heirloom Collage and started taking commissions. Now, she offers an online course that guides participants in producing their own artist-quality collages out of kiddos’ creations. The course consists of six video modules totaling one hour, and Blakley provides feedback in a private Facebook group where students can post their in-progress and completed work. Molly Revers enjoys dabbling in different artistic endeavors, so she signed up for the $99 e-course. “The most meaningful aspect was the joy it brought me when creating the collages and the joy it brought my little grandsons when they saw their work displayed in such a cool way,” she shared. “They love picking their favorite creations and memories associated with them.” Heirloom Collage Another parent’s completed collage For Blakley, who lives in Richmond, Virginia, and began her career as a fine artist over a decade ago, the project reconnected her to a sense of spontaneity after a period of creative stagnation. “Halfway through it, I recall thinking, ‘[My kids] didn’t second-guess their creativity in these pieces, so I shouldn’t either,’” she said. “That was a big breakthrough for me.” It’s something many adults, artists or not, can relate to. “A lot of my students haven’t made art since they were kids, and this brings them back to it,” Blakley added. Overall, though, the memorable shared experience of making that first collage with her two children — the youngsters helped select the included drawings and “were buzzing with pride” — is what she wishes for her clients. “That connection is what lasts, and they end up with something their family really treasures,” she said. Heirloom Collage Jeanine Long-Tuohy with her granddaughter Ava and the collage they made Jeanine Long-Tuohy, who loves her granddaughter Ava’s artwork, created her first piece with Ava’s help and has since started a new one with another grandchild. “Working on this made me feel like there’s a lot more we can do together,” Long-Tuohy said. “It’s a memory they will always have of me.”

Όπως και στη νέα σειρά AKKA, για αιώνες, πολλές οικογένειες Nair ακολούθησαν ένα μοναδικό μητρογραμμικό σύστημα που ονομάζεται Marumakkathayam, όπου η οικογενειακή ταυτότητα και η κληρονομιά περνούσαν από την πλευρά της μητέρας. Ακόμη και ο γιος ενός βασιλιά δεν μπορούσε να κληρονομήσει τον θρόνο. Πήγε στον γιο της αδερφής του!…
items.descriptionOriginal: In Kerala, your father’s property could belong to your aunt’s children! Just like in the new series AKKA, for centuries, many Nair families followed a unique matrilineal system called Marumakkathayam, where family identity and inheritance passed through the mother’s side. Even a king’s son could not inherit the throne. It went to his sister’s son! But here’s the twist: women passed down the family name, while men, especially the eldest maternal uncle, held the power. The system was abolished in 1975, but matrilineal traditions continue in parts of India. items.descriptionOriginal: In Bajaura, in Himachal Pradesh's Kullu district, farmers have had to rethink their orchards twice. As changing weather made apple cultivation harder, they turned to pomegranates. Then plant viruses began affecting those orchards too. Now, persimmons are offering another possibility. For anyone who associates Himachal with bags of apples brought home after a holiday, that change may be surprising. For the people tending these orchards, it comes down to a pressing question: what can they grow to keep earning from their land? Rising temperatures, declining snowfall and unpredictable rainfall are making familiar crops harder to rely on. Farmers are responding by trying different fruits, growing crops together and changing how they care for their soil. Their efforts feature in a study by the Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW), supported by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD). Released on 31 October 2026, it draws on experiences across 12 gram panchayats in Mandi, Kullu, Sirmaur and Shimla . The study identifies 25 ways communities can prepare for climate risks. Among them are practices villagers have already begun putting to work, shaped by what they see happening in their fields and around their homes. What do you plant when the familiar crop struggles? Bajaura's move towards persimmons shows how much adjustment farming now demands. Replacing apples with pomegranates did not end the uncertainty. Farmers had to look for another option when disease affected the replacement crop. Growing a mix of crops can help spread the risk of a poor harvest, though poor transport and limited cold storage still constrain farmers' earnings. Photograph: (Himachal Watcher) And choosing a fruit is only part of making an orchard viable. Farmers need water to grow it and roads to get the harvest to buyers. In Bajaura, dwindling irrigation water and roads damaged during disasters continue to make both difficult. In Parara, Sirmaur, growers face a related problem. Residents report that changing rainfall and rising temperatures have altered planting schedules and increased diseases affecting tomatoes and garlic. Some farmers are combining garlic cultivation with specialised apple varieties . The village's efforts also include natural farming and rainwater harvesting. Growing a mix of crops can help spread the risk of a poor harvest, though poor transport and limited cold storage still constrain farmers' earnings. For a farming household, finding something that grows is the beginning. Being able to sell it is what helps pay the bills. In Sandhu, change begins with the soil In Sandhu, Shimla, farmers are reconsidering how they grow their crops. Community members report that prolonged chemical fertiliser use has affected soil quality and fertility. Local women have responded by taking up natural farming, which avoids synthetic fertilisers and pesticides and uses resources available on the farm. The aim is to nurture the soil while reducing reliance on purchased chemical inputs . According to community accounts documented in the study, the practice has spread to more than 20 families after residents found it profitable and better able to withstand extreme weather. That experience gives neighbours something practical to consider: a different way of farming already being tried close to home. Yet even healthier soil and a different crop need water. In nearby Sirmaur district, that has brought women's groups back to the traditional sources their villages once relied on. Bringing water back to village life Thana Kashoga once had 35 perennial baoris, traditional spring-fed water structures that supplied households throughout the year. According to the study, only 10 remain. Residents report declining rainfall and rising temperatures , putting increasing pressure on these sources. The shortage reaches into everyday life, affecting drinking water, irrigation and livestock. Fodder scarcity and forest fires have also made pastoral livelihoods harder to sustain. Local women have responded by taking up natural farming, which avoids synthetic fertilisers and pesticides and uses resources available on the farm. The aim is to nurture the soil while reducing reliance on purchased chemical inputs. Photograph: (Triya Gulati via The Print) Women's groups have taken on the work of maintaining and restoring the baoris. Their efforts connect directly to what farmers are trying to do: keep village life possible as the conditions supporting it change. These communities still need dependable irrigation, transport and support to carry their work forward. A new crop cannot fix a damaged road, and a restored water source needs continued care. But in Thana Kashoga, there is a tangible reason to keep going. Women's groups clean the baoris monthly. Five springs have been revived, with work on another five or six under way. Sources: 'Villages in Himachal adapting climate change with new crops, revived springs' : By Shailee Dogra, Published on 1 November 2026 'How can Himalayan communities anticipate risks and adapt to a changing climate? Evidence from 12 Gram Panchayats of Himachal Pradesh' : By Ahana Chatterjee, Meet Kumar, Srishti Mandal, Taveri Rajkhowa, and Shreya Wadhawan, Published on 31 October, 2026

items.descriptionOriginal: For a five-year-old, changing schools can mean more than walking into a new classroom or learning a different routine. It can also mean leaving behind familiar faces, favourite teachers and friends who have been part of their everyday lives. Four months after her daughter moved to a new school, Shivani Tyagi decided to revisit the experience with a simple question: "When we changed your school, how did you feel?" Her daughter's answer caught her attention. "It was very upsetting," she said, explaining that the hardest part was leaving her friends behind. She hadn't wanted to do that. Even after settling into a new school, children may need time and space to process the emotions of leaving old friends behind. Rather than brushing aside the response or reassuring her that everything was fine, Shivani chose to listen and ask her daughter more about how she had managed the change. Making room for difficult feelings Shivani, a certified nutritionist, parent coach and NLP coach, believes that children do not always express what they are feeling immediately. Sometimes, they need time, reassurance and a comfortable space to put their emotions into words. Her daughter had settled into the new school, made friends and appeared to be adjusting well. But Shivani wanted to understand what the transition had felt like from her daughter's perspective. When she asked how she had managed the move despite finding it upsetting, her daughter explained that she was willing to try. Having the space to express what she was feeling made it easier for her to navigate the change. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Shivani Tyagi - Parent coach, Nutritionist, NLP practitioner (@parenting_with_shivani) For Shivani, that was a moment of pride. She was happy to see her daughter acknowledge that something had been difficult while still finding the courage to give a new environment a chance. She also understood that making new friends did not mean forgetting the old ones. They could still stay in touch with their previous classmates while gradually building new friendships. Keep asking, even after they seem settled School transitions can bring a mix of emotions for young children. Excitement about a new classroom may exist alongside sadness about leaving familiar surroundings. And just because a child appears comfortable after a few weeks does not necessarily mean they have processed everything. This is why Shivani makes it a habit to have open conversations with her daughter about everyday experiences, whether big or small. For parents navigating a similar transition, the approach need not be complicated. A simple conversation over dinner, during a bedtime routine or on the way back from school can create an opportunity for children to share what is on their minds. Simple everyday conversations can help children feel safe expressing emotions they may otherwise struggle to put into words. Instead of immediately offering solutions, parents can begin by asking what they miss, what they enjoy about the new school or whether anything has been difficult. The idea is not to have all the answers but to let children know that their feelings are welcome. Sometimes, a child does not need to be told that everything will be fine. They simply need to know that they can talk about what isn't. All images courtesy of Shivani Tyagi Source: 'Helping Kids Handle Change at School' by PBS Kids, Published on 11 January 2022.

items.descriptionOriginal: In South Sudan in 2024, just out of high school, Nyakangba Nelson Luka Poyo asked himself what kind of life a kid born in 2021 in Tambura would have apart from killing, hatred, bloodshed, and living in a camp. Amid tears, that question gave him his life’s purpose. He thought if young people had opportunities to learn and communicate, and the space in which to express themselves, they could realize alternatives to violence. He called it a “Peace Voice.” Young people make up an estimated 70% of South Sudan’s population, yet they have no voice. They are swept up into conflict at a shockingly young age. In a Peace Journey program, Nyakangba learned about Laddership, and how to become a “ladder” for others lifting them up through support and opportunities. Now, through Peace Voices to Vision, he helps young people “develop a common understanding of how to live together peacefully. Everyone deserves peace.”

items.descriptionOriginal: This article is published in partnership with Museum of Solutions For a child who has never used a computer independently, the first lesson in artificial intelligence isn't about algorithms. It's about a cursor. For one Grade 6 student from a government school in Maharashtra's Raigad district, that lesson began inside a 10-storey children's museum in Mumbai's Lower Parel, tucked into the old Kamala Mills compound: the Museum of Solutions (MuSo). When the student joined an immersive artificial intelligence (AI) learning programme there, computers were still unfamiliar territory. Even using a laptop touchpad and typing basic commands were challenges. But over the next few sessions, that began to change. By the end of the programme, the student had created an email account, learnt to use Microsoft Word and OneDrive, and taken part in coding challenges through Minecraft Education. What started with the basics of operating a computer had opened a door to exploring artificial intelligence, experimenting with technology and understanding how it works. "From day one, it was pretty interesting. The AI workshop at the Museum of Solutions brought teachers and students together to learn about technology, explore AI and understand how it can be used to find solutions to different problems, from those in our classrooms to challenges at a global level," says Meera, a student, who attended the workshop at MuSo. For thousands of children from underserved communities across Maharashtra, such opportunities are becoming a first introduction to the technology that is increasingly shaping the world around them. Students experiment with machine learning by training models to recognise objects and understanding how the information they receive shapes their results. Through AI Explorers, an initiative at MuSo, children are learning about AI through interactive games, experiments, creative exercises and coding activities. The programme, supported by Microsoft Philanthropies India and implemented by JSW Foundation, aims to make AI education more accessible to children who may have limited opportunities to engage with digital learning. Between July 2025 and June 2026, the initiative reached 9,087 children through foundational AI workshops, while another 313 students took part in a more intensive 10-hour learning pilot. It also trained 80 teachers and worked with 36 schools and 17 NGO and community partners across six districts of Maharashtra. But the numbers tell only part of the story. At its heart, the initiative is about making sure that a child's access to emerging technologies is not decided by the circumstances they grow up in. Bringing AI education beyond privileged classrooms AI is already influencing how children interact with the world, from the content they watch to the apps they use. But knowing how to use a digital device and understanding the technology behind it are two very different things. For children from underserved communities, opportunities to explore AI, experiment with coding or even use a computer independently can be limited. The data bears this out. According to the Ministry of Education's UDISE+ 2024-25 data, only 57.9% of schools in India have computers that work for teaching, and in government schools the figure falls to 52.7%. In Maharashtra, more than 25,000 of the state's 1.08 lakh schools, nearly one in four, had no functional computer. Children explore how AI works through interactive activities, learning to question its outputs rather than simply accept them. At home, the gap is wider still. The ASER 2023 'Beyond Basics' survey of rural youth aged 14 to 18 found that while about 90% of households had a smartphone, only 9% had a computer or laptop. Those with a computer at home were far more likely to know how to use one (85%) than those without (33.9%). Meanwhile, AI is arriving in classrooms. From the 2026-27 academic year, the Ministry of Education is introducing AI and computational thinking in schools from Class 3 onwards. This gap led MuSo to conceptualise AI Explorers. It's a natural fit for a museum whose very name is a mission statement. Opened in November 2023 by the JSW Group and founded by Tanvi Jindal Shete, a former Teach For India fellow, the not-for-profit museum aims to empower children to find solutions to India's most pressing problems. Within a year, it was named on TIME's list of the World's Greatest Places of 2024 and became the first Indian museum to win the international Hands On! Children in Museums Award, competing against 32 museums from 17 countries. "AI already shapes children's lives through the phones in their homes, the apps they use and the content they are shown. Yet children from underserved communities rarely get the chance to understand how it works, let alone question it," says Susan Vaidyan, Head of Education MuSo. The programme introduces students from Classes 5 to 10 to foundational AI concepts, machine learning, prompt engineering, digital literacy, coding and responsible technology use. Rather than beginning with technical explanations, the sessions use familiar examples and hands-on activities. In one activity, students use a teachable machine to train a machine-learning model to recognise different objects or images. They experiment with the data being fed into the system, and then do something unexpected: they deliberately train it incorrectly to see what happens. When the model begins producing inaccurate results, the children grasp an important truth about AI: its outputs depend on the information it learns from. The programme also introduces students to AI-generated creativity, prompt-based exercises and community problem-solving challenges, allowing them to explore how the technology can be applied to everyday situations. Microsoft's involvement brings technology platforms, learning resources and expertise in responsible AI to the programme. The programme introduces children to responsible AI use, including online privacy, misinformation, bias and cyber safety. "An inclusive AI economy cannot begin at college or the workplace; it has to begin in the classroom," says Kishore Kumar Thangavelu, CSR Lead, Microsoft Corporation India Private Limited. Through Microsoft 365, students learn to create email accounts, organise their work using OneDrive, write documents in Word and use Excel to organise information. They also explore Copilot to improve sentences, summarise information and help with everyday tasks. Minecraft Education and MakeCode introduce coding through play. Students programme a virtual agent to chop trees, build walls and construct structures using instructions, loops and conditional statements. The programme also uses Minecraft's CyberSafe world to introduce online safety through games and practical challenges. That matters: ASER 2023 found that nearly half of rural young people on social media didn't know basic safety features, such as blocking or reporting a profile. But the learning isn't limited to how these tools work. Children are also encouraged to question the technology, recognise its limits and consider when it should or shouldn't be used. AI Explorers began as a two-hour introductory workshop. But the team soon realised that children needed more time to move beyond demonstrations and engage with the concepts themselves. "It's important for children to not just use AI tools but to question their outputs and understand their limitations," says Susan. The 10-hour programme, spread across three days, gives children the time to do just that. They begin by exploring how AI and machine learning work, including the exercise where they deliberately train a model with incorrect information. On the second day, they explore agentic AI through block coding and a game that shows how AI agents observe their surroundings and make decisions. The final day focuses on responsible AI, covering privacy, transparency and bias, with examples such as deepfakes, phishing and voice assistants that struggle with different accents. Coding activities through Minecraft Education help students understand instructions, loops and conditional statements while learning through play. For Susan, the aim is to move children beyond watching demonstrations to experimenting, asking questions and recognising that a machine's answers are not always right. "They stopped watching and started doing: trying things, getting wrong results and working out why," she says. Their questions began changing too, from what AI could do to how it arrived at an answer, and when its outputs should be questioned. What changes when children get access? Over the course of a year, AI Explorers reached 9,087 children through its foundational workshops. Another 313 students spent more time with the subject through the 10-hour immersive pilot. The programme travelled across six Maharashtra districts (Mumbai, Mumbai Suburban, Thane, Raigad, Ahilyanagar and Pune), reaching children through 36 government and aided schools and 17 NGO and community partners. There was also an effort to ensure girls were part of this learning experience. Of the 7,398 student records collected, 54% were girls. That matters in a country where, ASER 2023 found, rural boys were more than twice as likely as girls to own a smartphone, and half the boys surveyed had an email ID, compared with under 30% of girls. But what did the children take away from these sessions? Between July 2025 and June 2026, AI Explorers reached 9,087 children through foundational workshops across six districts of Maharashtra. The assessments offer some clues. In the foundational workshops, 81% of the students assessed showed greater interest in AI, while 61% showed an improvement in AI literacy. Among the 126 students assessed in the immersive pilot, 80% demonstrated an understanding of AI and machine learning. Around 75% showed awareness of coding and cyber safety, while the same proportion had set up an email ID and accessed Microsoft 365, in some cases for the first time. For some children, the change was also visible in how they began to look at technology. At a Marathi-medium school in Mumbai, a group of girls initially felt that technology and AI were too difficult for them. But as they experimented with AI games and prompt engineering, they began creating AI-generated content, discussing ethical questions and using digital tools to explore sustainability challenges. What had once seemed out of reach had become something they could try, question and create with. From first steps to future dreams The Raigad student's journey offers a glimpse of what this access can make possible. At the start of the immersive programme, using a touchpad and typing basic commands were challenges. By the end, the student had independently navigated several digital tools, created an email account and taken part in coding activities. For Meera, it was a fun, experience-oriented way of learning, where she learnt about AI in depth through games and interactive activities. For children with limited access to computers, the programme offers an opportunity to explore technology, build digital skills and imagine new possibilities. "What I found interesting was that we were not just learning about technology, but also understanding how to use it safely and think about things like online privacy, fake information and bias," she adds. As Susan puts it, success is not simply about children learning to use AI tools. It is about seeing them experiment, doubt what a machine tells them and ask questions of their own. As AI becomes part of more aspects of everyday life, the ability to question it may prove just as important as knowing how to use it. And that is a lesson these children are beginning to learn early. items.descriptionOriginal: Every year, tonnes of paddy stubble are set on fire across Punjab, adding to the air pollution choking North India. But what if this farm waste could become something useful? For eight years, Gurdaspur-based innovator Parminder Singh experimented with paddy waste in his garage, even when people mocked his idea. His hard work led to an unusual innovation: drop-down ceiling tiles made using paddy stubble. Designed to provide heat and cold insulation, these tiles are also waterproof and fire-resistant. Through his startup, Agro Stubble Management, Parminder hopes to give farmers a reason to earn from crop residue instead of burning it. His vision is to establish production plants across Punjab, where discarded stubble can become a valuable raw material. items.descriptionOriginal: For 560 children at New Life School in Dharavi, Mumbai, the future of their education depends on one question: will their school continue to exist where it stands today? The preschool has been educating children in the neighbourhood for four decades. Yet, throughout its 40-year history, it has never owned the land on which it operates. Now, as Dharavi undergoes redevelopment, securing that land has become central to ensuring the school's future. An effort to help the institution do so has brought together an unlikely group: a 19-year-old college student, his friends and a community determined to preserve access to education for the neighbourhood's children. Taking on a fundraising campaign of this scale meant Daniel had to understand several areas beyond his college curriculum, including corporate social responsibility (CSR) funding, institutional philanthropy and campaign strategy. Daniel Gupta, a third-year advertising and media student at Mumbai University, is leading the effort through an initiative called Dharavi Rising. After raising Rs 22 lakh against an initial target of Rs 20 lakh for the school's expansion, the team has now set its sights on a much larger goal: Rs 1.5 crore to help the school secure its land and continue serving children in the neighbourhood. For Daniel, the initiative is about more than keeping a school open. It is also an attempt to change how people see Dharavi, a neighbourhood often discussed through the lens of overcrowding, poverty and redevelopment, rather than through the lives, aspirations and institutions of the people who call it home. And he is learning to take on this challenge while still attending college, without any prior fundraising experience or an established professional network. Building a movement around a school Daniel's connection with New Life School began through a friend whose parents run the institution. Learning about the school's four-decade-long journey also brought him face to face with a pressing question: how could an institution that had served generations of children secure a future for the next ones? "People are often surprised when they learn that this school has been running for 40 years without owning its land. We want more people to know that it exists and understand why securing its future matters," Daniel says. What began as an effort to support the school gradually took shape as Dharavi Rising, an initiative that brings together young people and the wider community to address the institution's long-standing challenges. For the teachers, the campaign offers an opportunity to draw attention to a school that has continued to serve children despite the uncertainty surrounding its future. "We wholeheartedly support Daniel's mission to secure the future of our school in Dharavi. We want to do everything we can to ensure that the children's education continues without disruption," say teachers Kelsi Rani Raja and D. Packia Hincy. For the teachers, the campaign offers an opportunity to draw attention to a school that has continued to serve children despite the uncertainty surrounding its future. Their support also reflects a practical concern for families who depend on accessible schooling. The team wants to preserve an institution that parents can afford, rather than see its future compromised by the changes taking place around it. From Rs 20 lakh to Rs 1.5 crore When Daniel and his college friends began working on Dharavi Rising in November 2025, the idea was to find creative ways for young people to contribute to a cause. Daniel was just 19 when he took on the responsibility of building the initiative. With no previous experience in fundraising or social-impact work , he had to learn how to approach potential donors, understand funding mechanisms and communicate the school's needs. The team's first fundraising effort set a target of Rs 20 lakh for the school's expansion. They eventually raised Rs 22 lakh, marking an important milestone for a student-led initiative. However, the initial achievement was only a starting point. The larger challenge of securing the land on which the school stands remained. View this post on Instagram A post shared by New Life School | Dharavi Rising (@new_life_school_dharavi) This prompted the team to launch Dharavi Rising 1.5, with a fundraising target of Rs 1.5 crore to help secure the school's future. The new campaign takes on a more ambitious, long-term challenge: ensuring that an institution that has educated generations of children can continue to do so. Learning to navigate an unfamiliar challenge Taking on a fundraising campaign of this scale meant Daniel had to understand several areas beyond his college curriculum, including corporate social responsibility (CSR) funding, institutional philanthropy and campaign strategy. "I had absolutely no prior experience in any of this, so I needed guidance. I realised there would genuinely be no better tool than ChatGPT," he says. Daniel had been using the AI tool even before starting Dharavi Rising. Like many students, he initially turned to it for help with college presentations and assignments. But as the initiative took shape, his questions became more specific. How does CSR funding work? What policies should he understand? How could he explain the initiative to potential supporters? What would a fundraising campaign need to communicate to people who knew little about the school? ChatGPT became one of the tools he used to work through these questions. "I used it to explore naming and branding ideas, work on campaign strategy , understand broad fundraising and CSR concepts, and develop outreach material. I also used it to identify website requirements and organise my thinking about how to present Dharavi Rising to prospective donors," he tells The Better India . The tool helped him break down an unfamiliar and complex task into smaller, more manageable steps. He also used AI-generated text in donor communications. View this post on Instagram A post shared by New Life School | Dharavi Rising (@new_life_school_dharavi) Daniel estimates that ChatGPT saves him two to three hours a day, helping him balance college with the demands of organising the campaign and communicating with potential donors. However, he recognises that AI cannot replace the judgement and effort required to run an initiative of this nature. He says he rejects suggestions that do not align with Dharavi Rising's objectives and is careful about the information he shares with the tool. He also acknowledges that he has not followed a systematic process to independently verify all the guidance generated by ChatGPT. Ultimately, the campaign continues to depend on people: the school staff who understand its needs, the families whose children attend it, the friends supporting the initiative and the donors willing to contribute. Keeping education within reach For New Life School's teachers, the central concern remains the children. The campaign is not simply about raising money for a building or an expansion. It is about helping secure the future of an educational institution that has remained accessible to families in the neighbourhood for four decades. The challenge now is to build on the team's initial achievement and reach enough people to support the school's longer-term needs. The challenge now is to build on that initial achievement and reach enough people to support the school's longer-term needs. For Daniel, the effort also carries a larger purpose: changing perceptions of Dharavi and highlighting the aspirations, initiatives and community institutions that exist within the neighbourhood. "My work with Dharavi Rising began with a desire to change perceptions of a neighbourhood. It has since developed into a concrete effort to help protect one of its educational institutions . Yes, AI has helped me navigate some of that unfamiliar territory, but the purpose of all our work remains rooted in the school and the children it serves," Daniel says, pointing at the colourful artwork-laden boards in the classroom where he was sitting during a conversation with The Better India . For the 560 children who attend New Life School, the goal is simple: to ensure that a school that has been part of their neighbourhood for decades can continue to be part of their future. This Children's Day, those who wish to support Daniel's efforts to secure the future of New Life School and its 560 children can contribute by visiting dharavirising.com and making a donation.

items.descriptionOriginal: Lafora disease is a rare genetic condition that typically affects kids and adolescents, causing frequent seizures and the gradual loss of cognitive function. There is no cure, so the focus for many parents inevitably turns to quality of life. That’s something Detroit mom Azeza Kasham was struggling to maintain for her 17-year-old son, Gigi Breadiy, earlier this year. He was diagnosed in 2019, just days after his older brother died of the disease. Kasham’s husband has his own health problems and isn’t able to work, and the couple has two younger boys as well, so she took on multiple jobs to pay off medical debt. Breadiy uses a wheelchair, and the family home wasn’t fully accessible, so caring for him was becoming increasingly difficult. She’d tried fundraising on social media, but still felt like she was drowning. A stranger she connected with online would be her rescue buoy. Josh Liljenquist is a Minnesota content creator with over 23 million followers. Many of his videos fall into the somewhat controversial random-acts-of-kindness genre, but the 28-year-old’s main focus is rallying tangible support for people in need. After learning about Breadiy, he posted footage of himself meeting mother and son in February. Less than two months later, a GoFundMe he launched for them had raised nearly $600,000. “It’s just completely changed my life, you know?” Kasham shared during a recent phone call with Nice News. “It’s enabled me to give Gigi everything he needs, but that’s not all [Josh] did. And that isn’t even the most important thing. He restored my faith in humanity.” In the nearly seven months since meeting, Liljenquist and Kasham have become extremely close. “She’s literally like my second mom,” he said, adding: “She keeps saying that I changed her life, but I think she changed my life more than I changed hers.” His own mother also speaks to her often, and even flew out to Michigan to spend time with the family. The women connected so strongly because they both know what it’s like to care for a sick child, and the financial toll it can take. For the first six years of Liljenquist’s life, he was in and out of the hospital. He has a genetic disorder called alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency as well as eosinophilic esophagitis, a chronic inflammatory disease of the esophagus. That background has led him to direct more energy into helping families experiencing similar situations. “I want other parents to not have to deal with the same thing that my parents dealt with,” he said. But his fundraising has benefited people in all sorts of circumstances: a man in need of a new roof, a couple facing homelessness, a woman hoping to open a permanent pay-what-you-can cafe. For Kasham, the support from Liljenquist’s felt like God had answered her prayers. He, too, felt a divine hand in their meeting. The fact that they belong to different religions was a moot point. “She kept asking me, ‘Well, you know, you’re a Christian person. I’m Muslim. Does that matter?’ And I’m like, ‘Oh my gosh, no, not at all,’” he recounted. “That’s the first thing she would ask me. And I said, ‘Why would that matter?’” Before the GoFundMe, Kasham had to bathe Breadiy in the garage because the shower wasn’t accessible. Now, the family has paid down debt and made upgrades to their home, including a roll-in shower, that allow him dignity and privacy. “He has his good days. He has his bad days,” she said, noting that his seizures have worsened in recent months. “But one thing he has that puts the biggest smile on his face is he has his own space.” You can donate to Lafora disease research through Chelsea’s Hope .

items.description: Αντί να κόψουν το DNA, οι επιστήμονες χρησιμοποίησαν ακριβή ενεργοποίηση CRISPR με στόχο φυσικά γονιδιακά πλήκτρα για να ενισχύσουν υγιή αντίγραφα των CHD8 και SCN2A σε οργανοειδή ανθρώπινου εγκεφάλου, αποκαθιστώντας τη φυσιολογική ανάπτυξη των ιστών και την πυροδότηση νευρώνων αποκλειστικά σε μεταλλαγμένα κύτταρα.
items.descriptionOriginal: Rather than cutting DNA, scientists used precision CRISPR activation aimed at natural gene "dials" to boost healthy copies of CHD8 and SCN2A in human brain organoids, restoring normal tissue growth and neuronal firing exclusively in mutated cells.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Top Phoenix Wholesale Cabinet Suppliers Compared by Price and Material Quality and Sustainability Reading Time: 5 minutes Top Phoenix Wholesale Cabinet Suppliers Compared by Price and Material Quality and Sustainability Contractors and remodelers working in Phoenix face the same problem: too many cabinet suppliers, too little transparency on what “wholesale pricing” actually means. This guide breaks down the top Phoenix wholesale cabinet suppliers compared by price and material quality so buyers can pick a source that fits their project volume, timeline, and budget without guessing. Finding quality wholesale cabinets in Phoenix without overpaying Phoenix’s construction market runs fast. Builders and flippers need cabinets in days, not weeks, and the difference between a supplier with real inventory and one that drop-ships on a six-week lead time shows up hard when a project stalls. The five suppliers below represent the range of options available, from local custom shops to national manufacturers, evaluated on product quality, service model, and fit for trade buyers. 1. Highland Cabinetry Best for: Builders, contractors, remodelers, and investors buying at volume Location: 3011 E Broadway Rd, Phoenix, AZ 85040; also serves Mesa, Chandler, Scottsdale, Glendale, and surrounding cities Products: Shaker, Euro, and Nano style all-wood cabinets; soft-close doors and drawers; dovetail construction throughout Standout: 20,000-plus kitchens in stock restocked bi-weekly; tiered pricing delivers 10% to 20% savings as volume increases Highland Cabinetry launched in 2018 specifically to serve trade professionals – builders, general contractors, handymen, and restoration companies – who need quality RTA cabinets without retail markups or long delays. Contractors sourcing wholesale cabinets in Phoenix from HCI get manufacturer-direct pricing, dedicated account management, and included 3D design renderings that speed up quoting. Delivery options cover job site drop, client delivery, and warehouse pickup. The tiered pricing model rewards repeat buyers, so per-unit cost drops as project volume grows, a real advantage for anyone running multiple flips or builds at once. 2. Premium Wholesale Cabinets Best for: Homeowners and trade clients seeking full-service design and installation in the Phoenix metro Location: Serves Chandler, Gilbert, Glendale, Mesa, Paradise Valley, Peoria, Queen Creek, Scottsdale, and Tempe Products: Custom kitchen and bath cabinets; also covers offices, wet bars, pantries, closets, and outdoor kitchens Standout: Over 100 years of combined design experience across staff; full consultation, hardware selection, countertops, and lighting available Premium Wholesale Cabinets is locally owned and has run operations across the Phoenix area for more than a decade. Their model leans full-service: clients work with an in-house design team – Eric Skinner leads ownership, backed by designers and installation specialists – moving from concept through install under one roof. Highlighted projects include the Dove Valley Kitchen Remodel, Harris Kitchen & Bar, and Brown New Build Scottsdale. Reviews consistently mention responsive communication and a team that listens before making any recommendations. It’s a stronger fit for clients who want guidance through the whole process rather than buyers looking to pull from existing stock. 3. Hardware Resources Best for: Custom cabinet makers, OEMs, and dealers sourcing hardware and functional components at scale Location: Headquartered in Bossier City, Louisiana; distributes nationally Products: Decorative and functional hardware, dovetail drawer boxes, vanities, cabinet hinges, drawer slides, organizers, LED lighting, sinks, and linear moulding Standout: 140 patents filed; part of Dimora Brands, operating across cabinet hardware, door hardware, faucets, and accessories Hardware Resources has been in business since 1990 and employs around 201 people. It doesn’t sell finished cabinets. The company’s focus is the components and hardware that cabinet makers and dealers build around, so it fills a different need than full-cabinet suppliers. Trade buyers who fabricate their own boxes, or who need a consistent hardware supplier across multiple projects, will find the product catalog deep. Acquired by Harbour Group in 2010, it now operates under the Dimora Brands umbrella, which spans several related product categories. 4. Decore-ative Specialties Best for: Cabinetmakers and industry professionals sourcing custom doors, drawer fronts, and RTA components in volume Location: Monrovia, CA headquarters; manufacturing in Irwindale, CA; Elk Grove, CA; and Monroe, NC Products: RTA cabinets, doors, drawer fronts, drawer boxes, moldings, accessories, finishing, and hardware in wood, plywood, 3D laminate, and melamine Standout: Founded 1965; ranked 68th on the FDMC 300 list of top North American wood products producers; fast ordering software Decore-ative Specialties has manufactured cabinet components since 1965 and employs between 501 and 1,000 people across three production facilities. Their ordering platform lets cabinetmakers spec and order ready-to-assemble frameless components with a six-working-day ship window, faster than most made-to-order competitors. The company holds U.S. Green Building Council membership and won a WMIA Wooden Globe Award for Innovator of the Year in 2016 for a CNC sander shaper capable of producing 500 doors per day. Shipping from California adds lead time for Phoenix-area buyers, but the component depth and production scale make it worth considering for larger orders. 5. Premium Wholesale Cabinets of Arizona Best for: Phoenix metro homeowners and contractors who want custom cabinetry with financing options Location: Serves Phoenix metro including Chandler, Gilbert, Mesa, Scottsdale, Tempe, Glendale, Peoria, and Queen Creek Products: Custom kitchen and bath cabinets, closets, wet bars, outdoor kitchens, pantries, and offices; countertops and hardware included Standout: Featured in Phoenix Home & Garden and LUX Magazine; financing available; over 100 years of combined team design experience Premium Wholesale Cabinets of Arizona is locally owned and operated, with a decade-plus track record in the Phoenix market. The team – owner Eric Skinner, designers Michael and Brianna, and installation specialists Ralph and Billy – takes projects from design consultation through final install. Case studies on their site include the Mountain Residence and Harris Kitchen & Bar builds. The financing option sets this company apart from most wholesale suppliers, making it accessible to homeowners who aren’t paying fully out of pocket. Coverage across nine Phoenix-area cities means most metro projects fall within their service footprint. What separates cheap from quality in wholesale cabinet suppliers Price alone doesn’t tell the full story when comparing Phoenix wholesale cabinet suppliers by price and material quality. The construction matters more than the finish. All-wood boxes with dovetail joinery and soft-close hardware hold up through years of daily use; particleboard carcasses with stapled corners don’t, regardless of how good the door looks. Lead time is the second variable most buyers underweight. It matters. A supplier quoting an attractive per-unit price on a six-week lead can cost more in carrying costs and delayed closeouts than a slightly pricier source with stock already on the shelf. Phoenix’s build pace is fast, and inventory availability is a real differentiator. And the service model matters. Trade buyers running multiple projects benefit from dedicated account management and volume pricing, both of which reduce administrative overhead across the board. Full-service shops suit homeowners who need design help and one point of contact. Knowing which model fits the buyer’s workflow before committing to a supplier saves friction later. Sustainability and material choices in wholesale cabinets Sustainability is becoming an increasingly important consideration for contractors, builders, and homeowners comparing wholesale cabinet suppliers in Phoenix. Beyond appearance and price, buyers should consider where cabinet materials come from, how they are manufactured, and how long the finished products are expected to last. Cabinets made with durable materials can reduce the need for premature replacements, helping minimize material waste over time. Material selection plays a major role in a cabinet’s environmental impact. Solid wood, responsibly sourced plywood, and composite materials with low formaldehyde emissions are worth considering. Buyers can also ask suppliers whether their products meet recognized environmental standards, such as FSC certification for responsibly sourced wood or GREENGUARD certification for low chemical emissions. These credentials provide additional insight into material sourcing and indoor air quality. For trade buyers managing multiple renovation or construction projects , durability is another important part of sustainable sourcing. Features such as dovetail drawer construction, soft-close hardware, and sturdy cabinet boxes can extend product lifespan and reduce replacement needs. Choosing suppliers that maintain consistent inventory and offer reliable delivery can also help limit unnecessary transportation and project-related waste. When evaluating wholesale cabinet suppliers, contractors should look beyond claims of being eco-friendly and ask for specific information about material composition, manufacturing practices, certifications, and product durability. A supplier offering a combination of responsible material choices and long-lasting construction can provide better long-term value while supporting more sustainable building practices. Bottom Line The top Phoenix wholesale cabinet suppliers compared by price and material quality serve meaningfully different buyers. Volume-focused contractors benefit most from sources with real inventory, tiered pricing, and fast turnaround. Custom shops and full-service providers fit homeowners or smaller projects where design support and installation coordination matter more than unit cost. Hardware and component specialists like Hardware Resources and Decore-ative Specialties serve fabricators rather than end buyers. Match the supplier model to the project type, and pricing usually works itself out. The post Top Phoenix Wholesale Cabinet Suppliers Compared by Price and Material Quality and Sustainability appeared first on Happy Eco News .
