Πέρασε περίπου μισή ώρα σε κάθε στάση δ…
items.descriptionOriginal: Daniel Te, an American artist living in London, has set his sights on sketching distinctive landmarks at the city’s 272 active Tube stations. The 27-year-old recently completed all 16 stops on the Victoria Line in a 10-hour sketching marathon, beginning with Brixton and concluding with Walthamstow Central. He spent about half an hour at each stop drawing something near the station. Daniel Te / SWNS “I think drawing landmarks helps create a more distinctive sense of what a place is exactly,” he told SWNS. “Seven Sisters was the most memorable, and I really like the origin story — it’s the symbol of the place, just seven trees in a circle.” Te said he was surprised by what he discovered, not having researched the stations in advance. For example, at Highbury & Islington, he spotted a green plaque marking where George Orwell used to live. “And that’s something that I never knew,” he remarked. Daniel Te / SWNS When he got to the final stop at Walthamstow Central, it was getting dark and hard to see what he was sketching. “I felt relieved, hungry, tired, and satisfied,” Te said. “It was fulfilling, and I really liked the journey.” And despite increasing costs of transport, his day of traveling cost him less than $10. Daniel Te / SWNS Te moved to London from Portland, Oregon, in July, inspired to explore European city planning. “One of the reasons why I started doing Tube sketching is that I wanted to see more of London and have an excuse to go out and about,” he explained, adding, “I really do love the process of just exploring every single destination.” He has visited many cities, including Amsterdam, Vienna, and Prague, and has completed drawings of Berlin’s S7 S-Bahn and the Palace of Culture and Science in Warsaw. Whenever he sketches, he likes that people come and talk to him, share their own art, or simply watch him in action. Daniel Te / SWNS Next up? Te is inviting fellow Londoners to join him at Farringdon Station at 11 a.m. tomorrow to begin sketching the Circle Line. And further down the line (pun intended), he plans to turn the sketches into a book or expand his work to cover other locations. This article was originally written by Tahira Amini for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM For decades, wastewater treatment plants have been filtering out bacteria, chemicals, and biological waste before discharging treated water back into the environment. Microplastics have been going straight through. This week, a plant in Atlantic City, New Jersey, became the first in the world to do something about that, installing a system built specifically to capture microplastics before they reach the ocean. As of this moment, no law requires this. PolyGone Systems , a startup founded by two former Princeton University graduate students, built it anyway. Why microplastics are hard to remove Plastics don’t biodegrade; they break down into tinier and tinier fragments called microplastics, which don’t go away and build up in living organisms over time. Standard wastewater treatment removes a lot, but it wasn’t designed for particles this small or this plentiful. They get into the water from industrial discharge, stormwater picking up particles shed from car tires, and washing machines releasing microfibers from synthetic clothes. By the time water arrives at a treatment plant, the microplastics are already in it. “We’re discharging to the ocean,” said Matt DeNafo, president of the Atlantic County Utilities Authority. “So, if we’re not removing the plastic that’s in our wastewater, we’re putting it back into the environment. It’s getting into the fish that we’re eating, even the water that we’re bathing. So, it really becomes an issue for human health.” Microplastics and nanoplastics have already turned up in human bloodstream, brain tissue , and other organs. Some researchers have linked exposure to a higher risk of heart attack or stroke, though scientists are still working out exactly what harm these particles cause at different levels of exposure. How the technology works PolyGone’s founders, Nathaniel Banks and Yidian Liu , trained as architects, and the technology they built shows it. Their system, called Polypods, doesn’t try to filter microplastics out of water the conventional way. Instead, it replicates the surface of ultrahydrophobic plants found in wetlands, which microplastics cling to naturally. Scale that up, and you can pull microplastics out of a water stream with very little material and minimal energy. The lab numbers are strong: more than 98 percent of microplastics removed. There’s no commercial data yet, but Banks and Liu say the Polypods work best on the smallest particles, which are also the hardest to catch by other means and the ones most easily absorbed by living tissue. Liu on the design philosophy: “We really like how some sleek products such as the iPhone were able to resolve very complex problems with very simple but sleek-looking designs. And we want to really emphasize that in how we design the Polypods.” “I think this really marks a new era for treatment innovation, where we’re able to build very large, scalable systems that use a very small amount of material and very low energy to treat very challenging contaminants,” Banks said. “And, having the first system in the world for that in Atlantic County, it’s quite unusual.” Where PolyGone goes from here A similar installation is already running at a wastewater plant in California, and PolyGone is developing a residential version. The Atlantic City system was fully funded by a federal grant, and both the technology and the funding route could give other municipalities a path to act without waiting on a mandate. Του ρ…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM If you’ve noticed more spiders lately, near window frames, behind boxes in the garage, lurking in basement corners, you’re not imagining it. Fall is mating season for spiders , which makes them more active than usual, and when temperatures drop, many of them make the same call you would and head inside. Of the roughly 3,700 spider species in the United States, only about 0.3 percent are dangerous to humans. The rest are, in the words of Oregon State University Extension horticulturist Brooke Edmunds , “minding their own business.” Two things converging in the spiderverse It’s not only the cold driving these arachnids indoors. Spiders like cellar spiders, wolf spiders, and hobo spiders move indoors as temperatures fall, and once inside, many are also looking for mates and somewhere quiet to leave their eggs . “Just like us, they’re coming inside to get warm,” Edmunds explains. “They aren’t aggressive toward people, not even the spiders.” Some females carry egg sacs on their bodies; others are hunting for corners, furniture undersides, the back of a closet, anywhere spider silk can hold a sac in place. That’s part of why fall can feel like a sudden invasion when it’s really just two instincts running in parallel. What makes your home The Destination Some of it is biology, and some of it is a gap in the garage door seal. If the weather strip at the bottom is worn or the door doesn’t sit flush, that’s an open invitation. Same goes for cracks along the foundation and gaps around window frames. And if your house already has gnats, flies, aphids, or termites, spiders will follow, because those critters happen to make up a great menu for our eight-legged friends. Outside, what’s close to the house does a lot of the inviting. Colorado State University’s entomology experts recommend clearing away rock piles, wood stacks, old boards, and compost heaps from around the perimeter. Spiders go for dark, damp, undisturbed spots. Tree limbs that touch or hang near windows are another way in, and crawl spaces packed with boxes are definitely attractive to them. How to keep them out Caulking cracks in your foundation and making sure screens and door seals are intact does a lot. Fall is also a good time to go through basements, garages, and closets, not for tidiness, but because those neglected corners are exactly what spiders are looking for. If you’re digging into old cardboard boxes or boots that haven’t moved since last winter, wear gloves. Spiders have sometimes made a cozy home inside them. If you’d rather not evict the ones already there, that’s fine too. They’re eating the insects you’d otherwise be swatting at, and most will move on once the season turns anyway. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Can Today’s Construction Firms Make Their Operations More Sustainable? Reading Time: 5 minutes How Can Today’s Construction Firms Make Their Operations More Sustainable? When you envision a typical construction site, you likely picture roaring diesel engines, towering waste bins and clouds of dust. However, forward-thinking builders are proving that heavy-duty work doesn’t have to create heavy pollution. While traditional operations take a massive toll on the planet through emissions and discarded scrap, you can drive real change on the ground. By embracing thoughtful equipment care, cleaner energy and circular material sourcing, your crews can build a greener world from the ground up. 1. Prioritizing Low-Emissions and Salvaged Materials Every major construction project begins with a blueprint, but the materials you specify in those early drawings dictate your build’s lifetime environmental footprint. Traditional supplies like standard Portland cement and virgin structural steel carry staggering amounts of embodied carbon—the hidden greenhouse gas emissions generated during raw material extraction, manufacturing, and transport. Many firms are swapping out carbon-intensive staples for lower-impact alternatives that still perform reliably. Mass timber, sustainably harvested from certified forests, sequesters atmospheric carbon right inside a building’s frame. Meanwhile, opting for supplementary materials, such as ground granulated blast-furnace slag — a recycled industrial by-product that can replace part of the cement in concrete — can significantly undercut the carbon emissions of traditional concrete mixes. Sustainability also means keeping things local and circular. By sourcing reclaimed lumber, crushed stone and recycled structural steel from regional deconstruction projects, you eliminate the fuel burned shipping heavy freight across the country. Salvaging high-quality elements prevents unnecessary virgin extraction, reduces procurement costs and gives historic materials a useful second life. 2. Adopting Proactive Machinery Maintenance to Reduce Waste and Boost Efficiency A truly sustainable jobsite isn’t just about what’s being built, but also about how efficiently machines run while building it. Proactive heavy equipment care is an essential pillar of low-impact construction. When diesel-powered machinery operates at peak mechanical efficiency, engines encounter less drag, burn significantly less fuel and prevent harmful oil leaks from threatening surrounding soil and local waterways. Routine inspections and precision adjustments prevent premature component breakdowns, keeping bulky metal and synthetic assemblies out of scrap heaps. Daily cleanings with a pressure washer clear away packed dirt and rocks that strain the undercarriage rollers, while maintaining proper track sag prevents engine strain and reduces excess fuel consumption. For example, checking the rubber tracks on skid steers to avoid wear and tear while encouraging optimal performance through proper tension reduces engine strain from overly tight tracks. Doing so means saving fuel and protecting components, leading to fewer emissions and a longer lifespan, which reduces manufacturing footprints. Prioritizing consistent preventive maintenance across excavators and loaders also curbs project delays and saves expenses. 3. Cutting Site Waste Through Circular Construction Practices Traditional construction projects generate mountains of debris, but progressive firms are more often viewing discarded materials as valuable future commodities. Moving toward a circular model begins with systematic on-site sorting, so instead of commingling off-cuts and packaging into generic roll-off dumpster bins, crews establish clearly labeled recovery stations for clean timber, scrap metal, cardboard and masonry. Processing materials directly where the work occurs can save significant hauling fuel and slash disposal tipping fees. Contractors often deploy portable rock crushers to break down clean demo concrete and masonry rubble on-site, producing quality sub-base aggregate to use for access roads, staging areas and sturdy foundation pads. When structures must come down, intentional deconstruction is replacing wrecking balls. Instead of demolishing older framing, crews carefully deconstruct timber and fixtures for repurposing in community projects or donation. Through active partnerships with local salvage yards and regional architectural reclaimers, firms keep large volumes of solid waste out of municipal landfills and help nearby communities access sturdy, character-rich, reusable materials. 4. Cleaning Up Fleet Power Heavy diesel machinery is a core part of commercial construction, but powering an entire fleet on fossil fuels carries a steep environmental and human price tag. Construction vehicles can emit substantial particulate matter and greenhouse gases, worsening local air quality while driving up fuel costs. Consequently, modern contractors are investigating ways to make fleet operations cleaner, quieter and more efficient. Electrification is leading this charge, especially among compact utility machinery. Battery-powered mini-excavators, electric wheel loaders and cordless hand tools deliver instant torque without generating smelly exhaust fumes or extreme noise levels. The shift to electric dramatically improves jobsite air quality, safeguards the respiratory health of on-site crews and earns goodwill from neighboring residential communities. Many larger diesel rigs cannot yet fully transition to electric powertrains, so operational discipline must bridge the sustainability gap. Establishing an automatic five-minute engine shut-off rule for loaders and haul trucks will reduce the exhaust fumes in the air while shaving gallons off daily diesel usage. Routine fuel tracking can ensure every engine runs at peak efficiency. 5. Leveraging Smart Planning and Modular Prefabrication Careful planning can make modern jobsites more efficient, with organized factory processes replacing crowded material storage areas. Modular prefabrication shifts significant building processes off-site into climate-controlled manufacturing facilities. In these organized plant environments, automated cutting systems reduce raw material scrap while optimizing usage down to the millimeter. Assembling wall panels off-site allows workers to recycle off-cuts and minimize on-site construction noise and dust. Simultaneously, modular construction eases neighborhood strain by slashing repetitive truck traffic. Instead of individual supply trucks trickling through local residential streets each day, preassembled building modules arrive in consolidated shipments. Digital project management platforms take this operational efficiency even further with advanced scheduling software accurately tracking incoming deliveries to ensure high-value lumber, drywall and delicate insulation arrive exactly when crews are ready to install them. As a result, there are fewer chaotic staging yards and likely a large reduction in expensive, weather-related material damage from heavy rain or exposure to damp ground. 6. Building a Jobsite Culture Around Everyday Sustainability Advanced equipment and green certifications certainly help, but authentic sustainability ultimately begins with people. Creating an eco-conscious jobsite means fostering a crew culture with daily habits that make resource conservation feel simple and worthwhile. The small decisions made throughout an ordinary shift quickly multiply across multi-month commercial developments. Simple operational swaps, like eliminating disposable water bottles in favor of refillable hydration stations and ditching single-use plastic wrap, drastically curb daily jobsite litter and establish an environmental mindset on the ground. Switching to energy-efficient LED lightbulbs in temporary site offices and encouraging shared crew transit foster an office and field culture in which eco-friendly choices become second nature. Sustainability-minded firms actively show their teams how these practical habits mirror broader everyday eco-friendly lifestyles. Incorporating simple sustainable living ideas into workers’ routines inspires tradespeople to make mindful, low-waste choices at home and at work. When crew members see company leadership genuinely backing these principles, green building becomes a shared source of pride instead of just a compliance task. Lay the Groundwork for a Cleaner Industry You can transform your construction operation into a more sustainable operation without overhauling everything overnight. True sustainability is an ongoing journey built on practical, everyday choices. By making each project cleaner, less wasteful and more efficient, you will make a tangible difference with every build. You hold the power to reshape the building landscape, proving that with each structure, you can construct a stronger, cleaner and more resilient tomorrow. items.descriptionOriginal: In the search for a sustainable alternative to today’s lithium-ion batteries, researchers often look to materials found readily in nature . And in the latest such advance, researchers in Spain have made a rechargeable battery that uses vitamin B12 as a catalyst. Vitamin B12 is an essential nutrient that the body needs for making red blood cells and maintaining the nervous system. The human body doesn’t naturally produce vitamin B12, and it is usually obtained from animal products such as fish, meat, and dairy. The food and drug industry cultivate bacteria that produce vitamin B12 for supplements and additives. The team from the University of Cordoba decided to put the vitamin to use in zinc-air batteries. Metal-air batteries are more sustainable than lithium-ion batteries, which rely on expensive critical minerals that are mined with an environmental and ethical cost. Metal–air batteries consist of a negative electrode made of pure metal such as lithium, magnesium, aluminum, or zinc. The positive electrode has a porous structure that lets in oxygen from the air, and a catalyst at the electrode triggers electrochemical reactions with the oxygen. “Precisely because it uses atmospheric oxygen, one of the battery’s active materials is not located inside the battery itself, thus significantly reducing its weight,” the researchers write in a paper published in the Journal of Materials Chemistry A . So metal–air batteries can pack much more energy by weight than conventional lithium-ion batteries. This makes them promising for applications where light weight is crucial, such as drones or medical devices. Indeed, small zinc-air batteries, the most practical among the different types of metal–air batteries, are used widely for hearing aids. turn your house into a battery The Cordoba team wanted to make a rechargeable battery using a biomolecule. They have previously made batteries with the protein hemoglobin and the enzyme catalase, which contain iron. This time they chose vitamin B12, also called cobalamin. The vitamin contains cobalt (III) at its core, which would be essential for electrochemical reactions. Vitamin B12 is a highly soluble vitamin. To make it stable inside a battery that operates with water-based electrolytes, the team fixed it to the surface of carbon nanotubes, which are microscopic tubes made of carbon atoms. Then the researchers incorporated the nanotubes into the air electrode of alkaline zinc-air batteries. The electrodes reached a specific capacity of 199.4 mAh of energy per gram, giving rechargeable batteries with high performance. And the electrodes worked in a cyclic fashion, allowing for a battery that could be recharged for up to 250 cycles. The performance is far from what is needed for practical applications right now, but the work highlights biomolecular platforms as “a high-performance and sustainable frontier for next-generation rechargeable batteries,” writes the team. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Paid Wildlife Photos Power the Citizen Science Conservation Borneo Villagers Now Run Reading Time: 3 minutes Two Borneo villages have banned hunting since a Brunei-based company began paying for verified wildlife photos, proving citizen science conservation can run for under US$1 per hectare a year. Borneo villagers use their phones to run citizen science conservation that is changing how wildlife is counted. In nine villages in Indonesia’s West Kalimantan province, people earn cash for photos of birds, monkeys, and orangutans. The program, called KehatiKu, turns everyday sightings into data that scientists can use. For some families, the money matters. Octavius, a 50-year-old farmer, earned about 4 million rupiah, nearly US$230, in a single month. He says the extra income helps pay for his children’s college. Borneo Futures , a nature technology company founded in 2015, designed the program. The firm is based in Brunei, and biologist Erik Meijaard serves as its managing director. A team of Bruneian university graduates checks every submission before anyone is paid. The model grew out of frustration with past results. A 2022 study in Current Biology found nearly US$1 billion went to orangutan conservation from 2000 to 2019. Over the same period, about 100,000 orangutans were lost. Meijaard argues that conservation needs faster, cheaper feedback on what works. One-off surveys give only a snapshot. Steady monitoring by local people can show how wildlife changes from month to month. Participants download the free KehatiKu app and upload photos, videos, or sound recordings of wildlife. The program pays for 73 species, including birds, monkeys, wild cats, and deer. Rarer animals earn more. A common bird earns about 5,000 rupiah, or roughly 30 US cents. An orangutan sighting earns up to 130,000 rupiah, about US$8. Each animal counts only once per day, and payments arrive in cash every month. The program covers about 200,000 hectares in Kapuas Hulu district, an area larger than New York City. More than 800 people have signed up as observers. Most are small-scale farmers who grow rice, cacao, and durian. Since its launch about two years ago, observers have submitted more than 350,000 records. About half have passed checks and been paid. Others were rejected as duplicates or as species not on the list. More than 350,000 wildlife records have been submitted, turning local observations into valuable conservation data. Photo courtesy of Borneo Futures . Top earners can make up to 10 million rupiah a month. A typical local job pays 2 to 3 million rupiah. For many families, wildlife watching now adds a steady side income without taking time away from farming. The money also shifts who holds power at home. Antonia Uneng, a part-time nursing assistant, says the project has made her financially independent. Her husband works abroad, and she no longer relies on him for every expense. Attitudes toward wildlife are changing too. Two participating villages have voluntarily banned hunting and trapping. Some villagers who once saw wild boar and deer as crop pests now want to protect them. Nardiyono, who directs Borneo Futures Indonesia, puts the logic simply. A photographed bird earns more over time than one sold or eaten. The bird also stays in the forest to breed. This is what makes Borneo villagers’ citizen science conservation useful to scientists. Borneo Futures uses occupancy models, which estimate how much of an area a species uses. These models account for animals that observers miss. Officials already use the results. Borneo Futures shared gibbon data with the Indonesian government for a national gibbon workshop. With community consent, it also plans to add records to the Global Biodiversity Information Facility, an open international database. Cost is another advantage. Meijaard says the program delivers results for less than US$1 per hectare per year. That is a small fraction of what many traditional surveys cost. Borneo Futures’ citizen science conservation also reaches oil palm plantations. On estates run by Indonesian palm oil company Austindo Nusantara Jaya, workers record wildlife during their daily tasks. A 2025 study found the data produced reliable occupancy estimates, despite its messiness. Orangutans and gibbons were much more common near large forest patches. Water monitor lizards turned up almost everywhere. Some workers now use fixed species lists and a phone app that logs each sighting’s location. Philanthropic foundations have provided about US$300,000 so far. Roughly half paid for the app and an artificial intelligence system that helps verify photos. Funding is secured through 2028, and two more villages are set to join soon. Outside experts are watching the citizen science conservation model Borneo villages have adopted. Paul Ferraro of Johns Hopkins University says the model likely outperforms top-down conservation. He warns, though, that people may drift back to old habits if payments stay low or enthusiasm fades. Meijaard hopes the approach could expand across Indonesia within a few years. That depends on long-term results and government support. If the numbers hold, communities built around citizen science conservation in Borneo could be copied in tropical forests worldwide. The post Paid Wildlife Photos Power the Citizen Science Conservation Borneo Villagers Now Run appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.title: Φανταζόμαστε τις ποώδεις πόλεις του μέλλοντος
items.titleOriginal: Imagining the Mossy Cities of the Future
items.description: Αυτή η ιστορία έχει εκδοθεί από κοινού από το Reasons to be Cheerful και το Outrider Foundation . Το 2012, ο Philip Wallisfurth ήθελε να σώσει ένα δέντρο. Πολίτες στο Άαχεν της Γερμανίας διαμαρτυρήθηκαν για τα σχέδια για ένα εμπορικό κέντρο που απειλούσε ένα δέντρο 150 ετών. Ο Wallisfurth, τότε ένας επίδοξος καλλιτέχνης του δρόμου, αναρωτήθηκε αν μπορούσε να χρησιμοποιήσει βρύα - αντί για τα συνηθισμένα του…
items.descriptionOriginal: This story has been co-published by Reasons to be Cheerful and the Outrider Foundation . I n 2012, Philip Wallisfurth wanted to save a tree. Citizens in Aachen, Germany, were protesting plans for a shopping center that threatened a 150-year-old tree. Wallisfurth , then an aspiring street artist, wondered if he could use moss — instead of his usual spray can — to support the campaign. He harvested moss from a local park, used yogurt as an adhesive and stuck two-meter-high letters onto the construction fence, spelling out “greener living.” The reactions surprised him. “People loved it,” he recalls. “Many took pictures and some spontaneously hung flowers in small vases onto the fence.” He had stumbled upon a medium that was soft, tactile and alive — and a natural way of occupying public space. YouTube tutorials suggested mixing moss with buttermilk in a blender, but the results disappointed him. Through trial and error with different mosses and yogurts, he developed his own approach to making “bio-graffiti.” Artist Philip Wallisfurth developed his own approach to making “bio-graffiti with moss.” Courtesy of Philip Wallisfurth Two years later, whiskey maker Jack Daniel’s hired him for a campaign. In Cologne, Wallisfurth covered an eight-by-eight-meter wall with moss lettering, spelling out a motto he lives by: never give up trying to do what you really want to be happy Now an artist with international projects and a studio in Berlin, Wallisfurth, 42, mostly paints large, colorful murals and designs anamorphic installations, room-filling works that seem to change shape depending on the viewer’s perspective. But moss continues to appeal to him for several reasons. He feels it’s uniquely suited to transform uninspiring urban spaces into places that feel more welcoming — and it has environmental benefits, too. He learned from speaking with scientists that moss can convert carbon monoxide and nitrogen dioxide into oxygen. “It also acts as a natural air filter and absorbs noise,” he notes. Moss continues to appeal to Wallisfurth for its ability to make spaces more welcoming and its environmental benefits. Courtesy of Philip Wallisfurth There are more than 13,000 recognized species of moss. The unassuming plant that most homeowners would like to scrape off their driveways offers more than unusual shades of green. It can retain moisture, dampen sound and, under the right conditions, help regulate the temperature of the surfaces it covers. Wallisfurth dreams of turning entire structures — for instance, train stations — into buildings where moss improves the air and atmosphere. As cities grapple with increasingly dangerous heat, Wallisfurth’s artistic experiments intersect with a serious question for architects and climate researchers: While concrete, asphalt and masonry store the sun’s energy, cities are searching for ways to keep buildings and public spaces cooler. Could this small, overlooked plant become part of the answer? Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Moss is remarkably adaptable. It has no conventional root system but absorbs moisture directly through its surface and can tolerate long periods of dehydration. A 2026 field study in Seoul showed moss-based green roofs reduced peak roof-surface temperatures by about 19° Celsius and maximum indoor temperatures by 2 to 3.5° Celsius during heat waves, while a 2026 peer-reviewed study from TU Delft in the Netherlands found that hydrated moss can produce evaporative cooling and insulate underlying surfaces. Credit: Lukas Gojda / Shutterstock Moss is remarkably adaptable. It has no conventional root system but absorbs moisture directly through its surface and can tolerate long periods of dehydration. It can retain moisture, dampen sound and, under the right conditions, help regulate the temperature of the surfaces it covers. As promising as these findings are, the reality is more complex than a green coating that simply cools whatever it covers. According to the Dutch researchers, the cooling effect only lasts as long as the moss is hydrated. Crucially, they found that dry moss exposed to direct sun can actually become warmer than bare mortar. So the question changes: Can cities engineer walls and roofs with moss that stays moist when cities most need cooling? Several startups are betting that the solution lies in redesigning the surfaces themselves. In London, Alive Labs produces moss-covered panels to turn city walls into living infrastructure. Founder and architect Nicky Naidu wants to change how the construction industry thinks about moss, which is often treated as a sign of neglect. “Moss gets a bad rep. But moss has intrinsic beauty, and we want to bring that beauty to cities,” Naidu told Reuters . “It’s carbon negative, bioreceptive, cost-effective and fire-safe. Everything that the industry needs and requires.” The company’s panels are made of a base material Naidu describes as bioreceptive concrete designed to support the growth of moss. The living wall systems incorporate controlled irrigation, delivering moisture directly rather than relying on rainfall or conventional surface spraying. Naidu argues that the moss walls are easier to maintain than conventional green walls because moss needs no soil to flourish. Alive Labs produces moss-covered panels to turn city walls into living infrastructure. Courtesy of Alive Labs In the Netherlands, Respyre has developed a similar concept with “Mosscrete,” a bioreceptive concrete that can be seeded with moss and also features an “ integrated, automated irrigation system that keeps the moss sufficiently hydrated, particularly during warmer and drier periods .” Both companies have moved from the prototype stage to making their panels commercially available. In Berlin, Green City Solutions built the world’s first vertical moss farm on 1,200 square meters to grow moss for sustainable air filters. The next step for the industry is to measure results in real life under varying temperatures and conditions, to determine where moss performs well enough to justify the investment. Not every experiment requires new materials or elaborate infrastructure. In Santiago de Compostela, Spain, a chance observation during the pandemic led city officials and university researchers to reconsider the vegetation growing between the city’s paving stones, including moss. After thermal cameras showed that stone surfaces with these small patches of greenery measured up to 25° Celsius cooler than bare paving, the city opted to leave the “urban microgreen” in place as a low-cost way to mitigate heat. A Respyre test panel after irrigation. Courtesy of Respyre Philip Wallisfurth keeps experimenting with the greenery, too. For a temporary installation, he transformed an entire living room in Berlin into an otherworldly moss-covered landscape. Again, he noticed people’s positive reaction. “The smell simply calmed people down,” he observed. “If you had a living moss wall in an office that was regularly watered, it would create an incredibly pleasant working climate. Plus, it filters the air and absorbs noise — it’s actually dreamlike.” Wallisfurth learned that most conventional moss art one finds in rooms is made from moss that has been dried and preserved with chemicals, eliminating the need to water it but also killing most of its environmental benefits. “It’s dead,” he says. His own bio-art has limits. Without preservation, the moss typically dries and dies within three to six months, depending on the surrounding dryness and acidity. “Like street art,” Wallisfurth notes, “it’s impermanent, too.” The walls of a bank building in Utrecht before and after renovation with Respyre’s bioreceptive concrete. Courtesy of Respyre But learning more about moss also made him reconsider where his material comes from. His sister, a nature guide, calls moss the “lungs of the forest” and told him it was wrong to take moss from forests and public spaces. He now sources his moss from an abandoned army training ground that is likely to soon be a construction site. His desire to create sustainable moss installations sometimes clashes with his clients’ expectations. Several big corporations approached him about creating moss pieces, he says, only to dismiss his concerns about sustainable sourcing. “They told me: ‘We don’t care. It just needs to look green in the pictures.’” He shakes his head. “That was a downer. It showed that most people only look at it as a means to an end.” The exchange captures a broader risk in the rush to make cities greener: The living material can become a visual shorthand for sustainability, even when its environmental value has not been proven. It might look green but actually be greenwashing. Credit: CinemaPhoto / Shutterstock “If you had a living moss wall in an office that was regularly watered, it would create an incredibly pleasant working climate. Plus, it filters the air and absorbs noise — it’s actually dreamlike.” –Philip Wallisfurth In addition to making his own moss art, Wallisfurth enjoys running moss workshops for kids at schools. Children love to experiment with the soft, tactile material, he says. Growing up in a rural part of the Eifel in Germany, he remembers walking barefoot across moss, and nature was his refuge when his own childhood was marked by loss. His parents died of cancer when he was young, and his brother was killed when Wallisfurth was only 14. He trained as a foreign-language correspondent and hotel manager before moving to Berlin and pursuing art. He turned to art explicitly as a means to brighten places up and turn rooms into positive spaces. “That’s what drives me,” he says. “Positivity is simply a much better way to deal with things. Of course, not everything is positive, but I have to try to stay positive.” His favorite projects begin with dark, inhospitable places and turn them into areas where people like to spend time. “That’s my goal as an artist.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime He believes he wouldn’t be an artist without his biography. And he sees a similar resilience in the plants: “A specialist once told me I could put moss in the oven at 270° Celsius, and if I water it afterward, it will come back to life.” In that way, he says, “Maybe I’m a little like moss. You can destroy it, but it simply grows again. It’s a fighter.” The post Imagining the Mossy Cities of the Future appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

Σε πήρα». Η γυναίκα καθοδήγησε τον Ρόγκαν από ένα προσγειωμένο αεροπλάνο, μέσω μιας πτήσης που ακυρώθηκε, σε μια νύχτα ξενοδοχείου και μέχρι την αγκαλιά της αδερφής της στο baggage cla…
items.descriptionOriginal: Thirty years after her mother died suddenly while she was serving in the Peace Corps, Kate Rogan still carries the memory of a stranger who met her grief with four quiet words: "Come with me. I got you." The woman guided Rogan off a grounded plane, through a canceled flight, through a hotel night, and all the way to her sister's arms at baggage claim - then disappeared, nameless, into ordinary life. What stays is not just the kindness, but what Rogan came to understand about herself in that moment: "I was this strong, independent young woman, but in that moment, I could not handle life without somebody helping me." Some losses crack us open in ways that expose how much we need each other, and some strangers seem to know this before we do.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How the Buffalo Return to Fort Peck Tribes Builds a Shared Future Reading Time: 3 minutes The buffalo return to Fort Peck Tribes restores culture, food, and learning in Montana. The buffalo return to Fort Peck Tribes is now one of the country’s longest-running tribal herd programs. In February 2026, the Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes received 219 bison from Yellowstone National Park. That shipment is the largest since the partnership began in 2012. It filled more than two semi-trucks, since each truck holds about 100 animals. The bison arrived at Turtle Mound Buffalo Ranch near Wolf Point, Montana. More than a dozen people waited in -13°F air. Buffalo once shaped life across the northern Plains. An estimated 30 million to 60 million roamed North America before the Civil War. By the late 1800s, only a few hundred remained. The last known hunt at Fort Peck took place around 1881. Buffalo then vanished from the area for almost 120 years. Program manager Robbie Magnan says buffalo and Native people were both pushed off their lands. That gap is now closing. The buffalo return to Fort Peck Tribes began more than 30 years ago, when the tribes set aside 5,000 acres. They bought 100 bison from Fort Belknap. Magnan says the goal was to reconnect culturally. Caring for large animals is costly, so the tribes built a business herd. Hunts and lotteries for public and tribal participants help pay for the program. Tribal elders asked for a stronger cultural focus. In 2008, the tribes split the animals into two herds. The cultural herd supports ceremonies, tribal hunts, food sharing, and education. The buffalo return to Fort Peck Tribes reflects a goal of cultural reconnection, with a business herd funded by hunts and lotteries and a separate cultural herd, created in 2008 at the request of tribal elders, supporting ceremonies, tribal hunts, food sharing, and education. Photo by Andrew Patrick on Pexels. Yellowstone faced its own problem. Its bison herd grew, and some animals wandered outside the park. Park managers once sent many of them to slaughter. The concern was brucellosis, a reproductive disease that can harm cattle. No case of bison passing it to cattle has ever been recorded. Still, the worry shaped park policy. The InterTribal Buffalo Council pushed for a live alternative. Fort Peck, Yellowstone, federal agencies, and the State of Montana then built the Bison Conservation and Transfer Program. It moves disease-free bison from the park to tribal lands. Rick Wallen, a former Yellowstone bison project leader, sees tribes as natural leaders. He says they have strong interest, deep cultural experience, and the authority to guide bison care outside the park. Fort Peck handles the quarantine step. Animals stay in four pens on 320 acres for one year. Staff test them under federal and state rules, and Magnan reports no brucellosis cases in the program’s history. The first delivery came in 2012, when 69 Yellowstone bison arrived during a spring snowstorm. Families from both tribes welcomed them. The arrival formally created the cultural herd. Once animals clear quarantine, the council helps decide where they go next. The partnership has sent bison to more than two dozen tribes in 16 states. The buffalo return to Fort Peck Tribes now helps other nations rebuild their own herds. Today Fort Peck cares for about 1,000 bison. The program follows state livestock rules and runs controlled hunts. It also reserves part of its herds for ceremonies and food security. Classrooms feel the change too. Each year, the Buffalo Unity Project brings Poplar Middle School seventh graders to the ranch for a bison harvest. Students learn anatomy alongside tribal history and culture. The Fort Peck Pté Group also drives learning. Formed in 2015, this group of mostly tribal women works with local schools on buffalo lessons. Member Suzanne Turnbull says the buffalo return to Fort Peck Tribes has brought pride and new economic opportunity. The group is also developing a buffalo trail lined with story poles. Turnbull describes it as a prayer path where families can visit the cultural herd. Tribal resolutions, foundation grants, and a National Endowment for the Arts award help fund it. The ecological payoff is clear. Conservation writers explain how bison grazing, seed spreading, and soil turning help grasslands recover. Turnbull sees the buffalo as a path back that also teaches people to care for all living things. See also: European Bison Reintroduction Restores Wild Balance in Romania’s Mountains Magnan hopes to grow the herd to 1,500 animals across 150,000 acres. The herd now stands at about 1,000. He wants the tribe to provide for itself again. What can other communities learn? The buffalo return to Fort Peck Tribes shows that patience, partnership, and local leadership can solve hard problems. Wildlife, culture, and the local economy can grow together when the people closest to the land lead the work. The post How the Buffalo Return to Fort Peck Tribes Builds a Shared Future appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM For more than a decade, residents in some of Los Angeles’s most densely populated neighborhoods have lived alongside oil wells: down the street from active drilling operations, near idle wells leaking methane, in communities where benzene and hydrogen sulfide from nearby extraction have been connected to higher rates of respiratory illness and reduced lung function. On October 28, the LA City Council voted to end that. The ordinance bans new drilling immediately, prohibits the deepening or redrilling of existing wells, and requires all active operations within city limits to phase out over the next 20 years. Los Angeles is now the largest city in the United States to ban oil extraction, and the first to kick the industry out entirely. A decade of community pressure It took more than ten years to get here, and Wendy Miranda, a policy director with Esperanza Community Housing , has been campaigning with STAND-LA , a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood drilling, for most of that time. “Front-line communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade,” she said. For Miranda, the campaign was personal as much as political. She and her mother both have asthma , and many of the communities closest to the wells are working-class neighborhoods of color where residents have absorbed the health costs of extraction for generations. “Frontline communities have been experiencing or have experienced for decades living near these toxic sites and having to pay for that with their health,” she said. California’s oil industry expanded rapidly in the early 20th century, when the state produced roughly a quarter of the world’s oil. Much of that production was in and around Los Angeles, and as the city grew outward, homes, schools, and businesses were built around the existing infrastructure rather than the other way around. Today, active wells sit near playgrounds, in residential neighborhoods, and along the coast. Idle wells, which under California law are those that haven’t produced oil for two years but can still return to production, dot the same areas. Residents near both report persistent odors, headaches, nausea, and breathing difficulties. The legal setback that opened a new door The City Council first passed an ordinance to phase out oil extraction in 2022, after sustained lobbying from residents including Miranda. Oil companies challenged it in court and won, successfully arguing that the city lacked the authority to impose a ban. California then passed legislation giving local governments broader power to regulate and restrict oil and gas operations. The October 28 vote is what came out the other side. Council president Marqueece Harris-Dawson was direct: “In South LA, working-class families have had corporations drilling across the street from their homes. No one should have to live near an oil drilling site.” The California Independent Petroleum Association has said it will challenge the new ordinance, calling it “an unlawful taking of private property” and arguing it will push residents toward greater dependence on foreign oil. The California Energy Commission has noted that the link between local production and pump prices involves crude costs, refining, transportation, and taxes, and that because oil is traded globally, domestic output doesn’t set what people pay at the pump. California’s production has been declining for decades in any case; output in the LA Basin is 43 percent lower than it was eight years ago. Who pays for the cleanup? The ban gets Los Angeles out of oil extraction, but what it doesn’t do is resolve what comes after. When wells stop producing, operators are legally required to remove equipment and plug them, but many haven’t. About 80 percent of idle wells in LA have been inactive for more than eight years, roughly a third for over a century. CalGEM, the state agency overseeing oil and gas, collected just $1 million of the $36 million in fines it was owed in 2025. A Carbon Tracker report found that even if all future profits from California’s oil companies went toward decommissioning, the state would still face a $7 billion shortfall. That gap falls to taxpayers. For Miranda and other advocates, the next phase is to compress the 20-year timeline and make the industry cover the cleanup costs rather than hand them off. She says she and her mother are both hopeful that future generations “can have better health and breathe cleaner air .” The council vote, in her words, “definitely represents hope.” Did this solution stand out? items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The morning shower is one of those things most of us have never really questioned. The alarm goes off, the water runs, and there you are, ready to start your day. Dr. Aderonke Obayomi , a board-certified dermatologist and assistant professor at Mount Sinai in New York City, has a word for it: habit. “A full shower every single day is a habit, not a medical requirement,” she says, and once you understand it that way, the whole ritual starts to look a little different. For a lot of adults, every other day or a few times a week is genuinely enough for both hygiene and skin health . For some skin types, the daily routine might actually be working against the very barrier the skin depends on to stay resilient. Why frequent washing can work against your skin Good hygiene and good skin health aren’t quite the same thing, and the difference matters more than most shower routines account for. “Hygiene is about removing sweat, bacteria, and odor,” says Obayomi. “Skin health is about protecting the skin barrier, the outer layer that holds water in and keeps irritants out.” Daily full-body washing serves the first without automatically serving the second. What the skin needs cleaned every day is targeted: “the underarms, groin, feet, and any skin folds,” says Obayomi. The arms, legs, and torso can skip the soap most days without any real hygiene concern. “Plenty of people can shower every other day, or a few times a week, and have perfectly healthy skin,” she adds. The reason hot, soapy showers can be hard on skin is fairly simple: they strip away the lipids the barrier depends on to hold moisture in and keep irritants out. Deplete those oils repeatedly, and the skin gets drier, more reactive, and more prone to conditions like eczema. If you work out daily, sweat a lot, or feel better starting the day with a shower, that’s fine. Just keep it short, keep the water lukewarm, and moisturize while the skin is still damp. Finding your personal shower frequency There’s no universal number. Dr. Pearl Ugwu-Dike, a board-certified dermatologist at Certified Dermatology , makes the case for going by feel over formula: “The bathing frequency should reflect your lifestyle rather than some arbitrary rule. Ultimately, skin health isn’t about how often you shower but about how well you preserve the protective barrier while keeping the skin clean.” Age changes the picture considerably. Infants can be bathed just two to three times a week: their skin is thin, still developing, and doesn’t generate much sweat or accumulate much dirt. Young children rarely need a daily bath unless they’re visibly grimy or have been in the water. Adolescents need more frequent washing as hormones drive up oil and sweat production. Older adults often find the opposite holds, since the skin produces fewer surface lipids over time, says Ugwu-Dike, which makes it more sensitive to the drying effects of frequent washing. Skin type shifts the equation too. For dry, sensitive, or eczema-prone skin, washing every two to three days with a fragrance-free cleanser and moisturizing each time thoroughly tends to work better than daily showering. Dr. Joel Spitz , a board-certified dermatologist and co-founder of Honeydew, recommends tepid water specifically for eczema: heat can worsen an already compromised barrier. For oily or acne-prone skin, the advice goes the other way: washing after sweating matters, because oil, bacteria, and sweat sitting on the chest or back can clog pores and make breakouts worse. Climate is part of this too. Hot weather means more sweating and usually calls for more frequent washing. During cold, dry months, shorter and cooler showers are gentler on the skin, and indoor heating compounds things by pulling moisture from the air all winter. A simple bedroom humidifier could help a lot too, says Obayomi. Signs your skin is asking for a break Your skin will usually tell you when you’ve overdone it, usually in the form of tight, uncomfortable skin right after stepping out of the shower. “That squeaky-clean feeling means you’ve stripped away protective oils,” Obayomi explains. Persistent itchiness at night or during the winter with no visible rash is often dry skin from over-washing rather than anything more serious. Flaking, rough patches, or a grayish cast, most common on the shins and arms, is another sign, and in deeper skin tones it tends to show up as ashiness. When the lipid barrier gets stripped repeatedly, Spitz explains, bacteria can get through to the deeper layers of the skin, triggering eczema flares and inflamed, sensitive patches. Small cracks or fine lines on the shins or hands signal that the barrier itself is starting to give. Signs your skin needs more frequent washing Body odor that lingers after changing clothes or applying deodorant means sweat and bacteria have built up past what a quick freshen-up can fix, particularly in the underarms and skin folds. Visibly greasy skin or hair is another clear signal. Breakouts on the chest, back, or shoulders, especially after sitting in sweaty workout clothes, usually point to accumulated oil and sweat clogging pores. Irritation in the groin, armpits, or between the toes can indicate bacterial or fungal infections that thrive in warm, moist conditions, says Spitz. Dark, scaly patches that look like accumulated dirt but don’t respond to a gentle rinse are worth a dermatologist’s assessment. Ugwu-Dike frames these signals well: “Some of these may indicate other health issues. Things to watch out for are persistent body odor, noticeable buildup of sweat, oil or debris, irritation in the skin folds, or an increase in body bumps.” Any of those may point to something that needs a dermatologist rather than just a schedule change. Shower habits that protect your skin barrier Frequency matters, but so does what happens inside each shower. Keep the water lukewarm and the shower short, ideally five to ten minutes. Hot water strips the oils you’re trying to preserve, and long showers pull moisture from the skin even when the temperature is reasonable. Use soap on the areas that need it: underarms, groin, feet, and skin folds. The arms, legs, and back usually need just a rinse, especially if your skin tends to run dry. A fragrance-free cleanser is one of the simplest switches you can make: “Fragrance is one of the most common causes of skin irritation and allergic reactions,” says Obayomi. Skip the loofah and stiff brushes entirely; a gentle touch does the job without the irritation. Moisturize within a few minutes of stepping out, while the skin is still slightly damp, to trap moisture before it escapes. Pat dry rather than rubbing, and make sure to dry thoroughly between the toes and in any skin folds where moisture lingers. For very dry patches on the hands, heels, elbows, or shins, a thin layer of petroleum jelly over your moisturizer holds in what a cream alone won’t. And if your skin stays itchy , flaky, or cracked despite all of this, Obayomi’s advice is to get a dermatologist involved sooner rather than later: “Ongoing dryness can be eczema or another condition that needs treatment. Treating it early also prevents dark spots from forming.” Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post The dermatologist guide to a skin-friendly shower routine first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Getting your daily steps in may be a little easier if you live in Hoboken, New Jersey. Earlier this month, Architectural Digest released a list of the nine most walkable cities in the U.S. based on recent studies, Redfin’s Walk Score tool, and consultations with realtors, residents, and tourism experts. The 1-square-mile city, which sits just across the Hudson River from downtown Manhattan, earned the top spot due to its ample public transportation and dense street grid. It received a 97 out of 100 on Walk Score, which measures the ability for residents to run errands and access amenities without a car — factors that can go a long way for physical health, mental health, and the health of the planet. View this post on Instagram “[Walkability] can benefit everything from household finances and health to the environment and overall quality of life,” Daryl Fairweather, chief economist at Redfin, told the outlet. She added: “Walkable neighborhoods also create more opportunities for people to interact with local businesses, use public spaces and resources, and connect with their neighbors.” Science backs up those benefits. A 2021 paper showed higher walkability was associated with lower mortality rates in a cohort of 13,832 women. And a 2020 study of over 31,000 adults found that those living in high-walkability areas were 150% more likely to engage in adequate levels of physical activity and 76% less likely to be obese. Additionally, research from 2013 suggested that participants who walked more in their neighborhood experienced improved social interactions and felt more social cohesion within the community. RELATED: How 11,000 Twins Helped Illustrate the Importance of Making Cities Walkable In terms of the planet, Elizabeth Sawin, director of the Multisolving Institute, a research organization focused on climate change, equity, health, well-being, and biodiversity, summed up the power of walkability in a 2024 interview with Grist: “Every trip taken on foot instead of by a fossil fuel-powered car reduces greenhouse gas emissions.” Here’s the full list of America’s most walkable cities from Architectural Digest : 1. Hoboken, New Jersey 2. West Hollywood, California 3. Boston, Massachusetts 4. San Francisco, California 5. New York, New York 6. Washington, D.C. 7. Chicago, Illinois 8. Miami, Florida 9. Philadelphia, Pennsylvania

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How 326 Fence Construction Helps North Texas Homeowners Create Private, Durable Outdoor Spaces Reading Time: 5 minutes How 326 Fence Construction Helps North Texas Homeowners Create Private, Durable Outdoor Spaces Key Takeaways 326 Fence Construction is based in Nevada, Texas, and serves Collin County and surrounding North Texas communities. Custom wood privacy fencing is a practical option for homeowners who want a more private, enclosed backyard. On-site measurements help account for slopes, gates, existing structures, access, and other site conditions. Fence cost depends on linear footage, materials, height, design, gate needs, and the property’s complexity. Wood fence performance depends on material selection, proper installation, weather exposure, and ongoing maintenance. For homeowners dealing with exposed backyards, aging fence lines, or properties that need clearer boundaries, 326 Fence Construction provides custom residential fencing solutions throughout Nevada, Lavon, Josephine, Farmersville, Princeton, McKinney, and nearby North Texas communities. The company builds wood privacy fences, metal fencing, pipe-and-steel fencing, ranch-style fencing, and custom gates tailored to each property’s use. A new fence should do more than mark a line between neighboring yards. It should support privacy, help define usable outdoor areas, and fit the home’s appearance and practical needs. During a consultation, 326 Fence Construction can review material choices, fence styles, gate options, and custom hardwoods requests based on the project’s budget, maintenance expectations, and layout. Considering these factors early can help homeowners choose a fence that suits their property and long-term plans. A Practical Answer to Backyard Privacy Concerns Many fence projects begin with a straightforward problem. Nearby homes may overlook a yard, an old fence may have loose boards or leaning sections, or a family may want a more defined space for outdoor living. A custom wood privacy fence can create visual separation while giving a backyard a finished, natural look. 326 Fence Construction approaches fencing as a property-specific project rather than a one-size-fits-all installation. Homeowners can discuss whether their priorities are privacy, pet containment, improved curb appeal, a secure gate, or a combination of these goals. The resulting plan can account for the fence line, desired height, style, and transitions around patios, sheds, trees, or changes in elevation. Local Service Throughout Collin County Based in Nevada, Texas, 326 Fence Construction serves homeowners and landowners across Collin County, including Lavon, Josephine, Farmersville, Princeton, and McKinney, as well as surrounding North Texas communities. Local projects can have very different needs, from a compact suburban backyard to a larger property requiring ranch-style fencing and a wider access gate. Planning a fence locally often means looking beyond the visible yard. Property owners may need to consider drainage, slopes, neighborhood or HOA standards, access for installation, existing landscaping, and the location of utilities. The owner-led business is headed by Clayton Dacey, whose background includes service as a police officer and whose company emphasizes clear communication and personal involvement throughout the project. Cedar, Wood, and Custom Material Choices Wood remains a popular fencing material because it provides privacy and design flexibility without losing a natural appearance. Cedar is a common choice for privacy fencing, while treated wood and other suitable materials may also be considered based on the design, budget, and maintenance plan. Important Factors When Choosing Fence Materials Privacy level: Board-on-board and closely spaced picket designs can provide more visual coverage than more open styles. Fence height: Height should support the homeowner’s privacy goals while complying with applicable local or neighborhood requirements. Exposure: Sun, rain, wind, and ground moisture can influence material and construction decisions. Maintenance: Wood fences benefit from periodic inspection, cleaning, and timely repair or refinishing when needed. Appearance: Top caps, trim, stain, and gate details can help a new fence complement the home and landscape. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Reducing Waste in Renovation Projects Can Be Easy: Just Apply These 7 Practices Reading Time: 4 minutes Reducing Waste in Renovation Projects Can Be Easy: Just Apply These 7 Practices Renovating your home can leave behind more waste than you might expect. Old cabinets, broken tiles, discarded flooring, leftover paint and piles of packaging can quickly add up. Much of this material ends up in landfills, even though some could have been reused, donated or recycled. However, a few changes in how you plan, shop and manage construction waste can make your renovation more sustainable and keep useful materials in circulation. Here are seven ways to reduce waste in your home renovation projects. 1. Plan Your Renovation Before Buying Materials Your renovation might involve just one room, but the materials you use still contribute to the construction industry’s environmental footprint. The buildings and construction sector contributes to 37% of global emissions and nearly 50% of global material extraction. You can reduce the resources your project consumes, including materials that might otherwise end up unused, by planning your renovation carefully. Before placing orders, measure each room and calculate how much flooring, paint and lumber you’ll need. Ask your contractor to help estimate quantities, accounting for reasonable cutting allowances and possible mistakes. This gives you a better shopping list and helps prevent excessive purchases. Design decisions are equally important. Finalize flooring, wall finish and cabinet style choices before construction begins. Changing these halfway through the project can leave you with surplus materials that no longer suit your plans. Coordination between you, your contractor and suppliers can keep purchasing on track. 2. Keep Existing Materials and Fixtures Where Possible Your home’s existing features might have plenty of life left in them. Keeping functional materials in place reduces the need for new products, which require raw materials and energy to manufacture and deliver. Take a good look at your cabinets, doors, flooring, countertops and plumbing fixtures before deciding what needs replacing. For example, a garage door with a standard torsion spring may last around 10,000 operating cycles. If it still works and its components are in good condition, regular maintenance could extend its useful lifespan. You can refresh outdated features with simple updates. Repaint kitchen cabinets, swap old handles, refinish hardwood floors or replace the bathroom vanity’s faucet. These changes can make familiar features look new again while keeping bulky materials out of the waste pile. Even retaining existing structural elements can prevent substantial demolition waste. 3. Choose Reclaimed and Recycled Building Materials Keeping existing building materials is a good start, but you can make your shopping list even more sustainable by choosing reclaimed and recycled products. They keep existing resources in circulation and reduce the need to extract and process additional raw materials. Look for reclaimed timber, salvaged bricks, recycled glass countertops, recycled metal fixtures and flooring made with recycled content. Architectural salvage yards and secondhand building supply stores are great places to explore. You might even find distinctive pieces that add character to your home, such as an old wooden door or vintage light fixture. Check the condition, safety and suitability of each material before purchasing. Reclaimed wood, for example, should be inspected for rot, pests and damage. You should also make sure recycled products meet the requirements for their intended use. 4. Store Leftover Materials for Future Repairs Extra tiles, flooring planks and paint cans could come in handy long after your renovation is finished. Keeping useful leftovers gives you matching materials for future projects, so you can replace a damaged section without purchasing an entirely new batch. Set aside spare tiles, grout, screws, cabinet handles, paint and flooring pieces. Keep them in their original packaging where possible and label everything clearly. Follow storage instructions carefully because products such as paint and adhesives may need specific temperature conditions. You may also need a place to store these supplies while construction is underway. A portable storage unit can hold renovation materials and other belongings away from busy work areas. It may also protect furniture and household items from dust and debris during renovation, reducing the risk of damage to your belongings. 5. Work With Contractors Who Prioritize Waste Reduction Your contractor has a big influence on how much waste your renovation produces. Their choices around demolition, material ordering and waste disposal can determine whether usable items are salvaged or thrown away. Before hiring someone, ask about their approach to construction waste . Do they separate recyclable materials? Can they carefully remove existing fixtures for reuse? Do they work with local recycling facilities or salvage organizations? These questions can help you understand how they handle unwanted materials. Discuss your waste reduction goals before work begins and agree on practical arrangements for sorting, collecting and disposing of debris. You can also ask contractors to track leftover materials and avoid unnecessary purchases. Clear communication helps everyone work toward the same goal. 6. Donate, Sell or Reuse Items That Are Still in Good Condition Some materials removed during your renovation could be useful in another home or construction project. Donating or selling them gives these items another purpose and reduces the demand for newly manufactured products. The EPA points out that reducing landfill waste can offset the environmental toll of mining raw materials and making new items from scratch. Look for easy-to-remove items such as doors, appliances and fixtures. You can offer them to local charities, secondhand building supply stores or people working on their own renovation projects. Working appliances and attractive light fixtures may also find buyers through online marketplaces. Other leftover materials can serve different purposes. Wood cutoffs can become smaller framing pieces, blocking or garden mulch. You can reuse crushed brick, masonry and concrete as fill, road base or driveway bedding. Even leftover paint can be remixed for use in storage rooms and garages, or used as a primer on another project. Before donating or repurposing the item, ensure its condition is suitable. 7. Reduce Packaging and Avoid Single-Use Supplies Renovation waste doesn’t come exclusively from construction materials. Cardboard boxes, plastic wrapping, protective films and disposable supplies can create another pile of trash before the actual work is finished. Ask suppliers about bulk ordering, minimal packaging and reusable delivery containers. You can also coordinate deliveries so materials arrive in fewer shipments, reducing excess packaging and transportation needs. Save sturdy cardboard boxes and packing materials to organize supplies or protect furniture during construction. For the renovation itself, choose reusable drop cloths, protective coverings and storage containers where practical. Washable cloths can replace disposable plastic sheets for many jobs, while reusable buckets and organizers can serve you throughout the project. Small changes to your purchasing and cleanup habits can prevent a surprising amount of waste. A Renovation That Doesn’t Cost the Earth A beautiful home and a lighter environmental footprint can go hand in hand. With some careful planning, material reuse and smarter waste management, you can make your renovation more sustainable at every stage. You might even find unique materials and creative ways to refresh your space along the way. Make your next home makeover one that looks good and wastes fewer resources. The post Reducing Waste in Renovation Projects Can Be Easy: Just Apply These 7 Practices appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Commonplace moments with a stranger can make all the difference in helping someone feel like they belong. You’re walking through the farmers market with a screaming toddler tucked under your arm football style. You’re tired, you’re leaving without the produce you came for, and you’re embarrassed. You pass by an older woman on the way out, steeling yourself for judgment. Instead, you get a knowing smile and hear, “We’ve all been there. You’re doing great, Mama.” And suddenly, you feel seen. Until recently, these sparks of connection didn’t have a name. Now, thanks to a University of Georgia researcher, they do: evanescent interactions. “What is communicated by these evanescent interactions is essentially, ‘You’ve noticed me. You’ve confirmed my existence. You’ve communicated that I am welcome here, that I belong here, that I have a place here, that I have value,'” says Joseph Hermanowicz, author of the publication and a professor of sociology at the University of Georgia. Hermanowicz defines evanescent interactions as brief moments when “strangers exchange gestures that create a ‘spark’ between them.” An evanescent interaction is more than just an ordinary exchange of pleasantries. These moments consist of brief but meaningful exchanges of mutual understanding and connection. “It’s important to be pleasant and kind to people, particularly in our present times, of course,” Hermanowicz says. “But I think it’s also important to recognize that when we do have a certain deliberateness with communicating with people, we could be accomplishing something very meaningful. We could communicate to people that they are important, that they matter, that we together form a community.” In his earlier research on the causes of undergraduate attrition, Hermanowicz found that evanescent interactions often influenced whether a student stuck it out or dropped out. Former students who dropped out says that a meaningful encounter with someone at the university who showed genuine interest in their well-being might have helped them feel more like they belonged. “In the absence of such contact, they felt alienated and not noticed, which fueled or did not impede a desire to leave,” he says. “So they left. “A lot of people are lonely. These sparks of connection can thwart feelings of not belonging in the various groups and organizations that we are a part of, whether those are friendship groups, work organizations, or society more broadly.” Evanescent interactions are brief, positive, and highly emotionally charged. They’re so ordinary that people may not give them a second thought. But they hold larger significance, Hermanowicz says. “Evanescent interactions are crucial to social life,” he says. “Two people communicating empathy to each other and recognizing each other as important holds extraordinary consequence. It affirms our mutual place in human community.” The article appears in Theory and Society . Source: University of Georgia The post How connecting with strangers can boost the sense of belonging appeared first on Futurity .

items.descriptionOriginal: Every geological epoch leaves signatures. One of the Anthropocene’s may be a noise. Oceans echo with the drone of ship engines and blasts of sonar. Cities and suburbs roar with speeding cars and revving motorcycles. Even remote wilderness hums with passing airplanes and strolling hikers. Humanity has turned up the volume on the whole planet. That soundtrack is far reaching. New research in Science finds that noise pollution more than doubles death rates among wild animals. It is also rewriting the rules of who eats whom. In noisy places, prey grow jumpy and predators go hungry. Sometimes an animal fleeing the din runs straight into danger. Noise, the authors write, “reshapes the acoustic arms race” between species, and it creates winners and losers. The researchers argue that protecting wildlife in the Anthropocene means protecting quiet. “This work shows that noise pollution is an underrated threat to wildlife worldwide,” said Hansjoerg Kunc , an ecologist at Queen’s University Belfast and the paper’s lead author. Soundscapes, he said, should be safeguarded with the same seriousness as forests, wetlands and other physical habitats. Scientists have long known that noise harms living things. The World Health Organization calls it a serious health hazard for people: it shortens lives, impairs children’s brain development and disrupts sleep. What was missing was the big picture. Kunc and Queen’s colleague Rouven Schmidt gathered 214 studies examining noise effects on 177 species across six continents, from tiny beetles to hulking whales. They focused on controlled experiments, which can more reliably pin effects on noise itself. The effects were widespread. Noise was tied to fetal deformities, weakened immune systems and elevated stress hormones. It altered body size, feeding and parenting, and it changed animals’ success at hunting or escaping hunters. Pooled across the experiments, noise raised mortality by 138%. If 10 in every 100 animals would die in a world without human noise, 24 would die in a world with it. That’s large enough, the authors say, to “threaten population viability.” The effects on how species interact may matter just as much. Animals tended to steer clear of noisy areas, so their numbers there were 37% lower. The prey that remained were on high alert. So predators in noisy places caught 25% less prey, even though they worked harder to find it. But noise doesn’t necessarily help prey either. A loud sound might send a prey animal into a burrow or other enclosed space to hide. Those close quarters can amplify the noise, and that can flush the animal back into the open, where a predator is waiting. The fix, the researchers suggest, starts with treating sound as part of habitat. Kunc points to “measures such as low-noise zones that give animals a genuine acoustic refuge.” In an epoch defined by human influence, quiet may be one of the habitats most worth saving.
